articles.title: Microsoft plays the Windows card in the AI game, with help from Nvidia
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft is turning to an old friend and a familiar advantage in search of a new edge in AI.
The company and its longtime partner Nvidia on Wednesday started taking orders for a new line of high-end Windows PCs built to run large AI models independent of the cloud.

Microsoft also announced what it calls “Windows Hybrid Intelligence,” a set of features that will let its Copilot assistant read the files on a PC, take actions on the machine and opt to run AI models locally instead of in the cloud when it makes sense.

It’s not a new concept to users of such programs as Anthropic’s Claude, Perplexity and OpenClaw, which already work with the files on a user’s computer. But only Microsoft can build the features into Windows itself, along with security controls that limit what an AI agent can reach on the machine and will keep a separate record of what the agent does.
“I think agents are going to be the largest users of the file system,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during an on-stage conversation with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at an event in San Francisco.

Microsoft got an early jump in AI with its 2019 investment in OpenAI and the 2021 debut of GitHub Copilot, its AI coding assistant. But its Copilot products for consumers and businesses have since been overshadowed by OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

Both rivals also moved quickly on AI agents that write code and carry out other tasks on a user’s computer, the kind of software Microsoft is now building into Windows. Microsoft’s own Copilot Cowork, which it introduced in March , integrates Anthropic’s Claude.

The tech giant has been reworking Copilot to catch up. Earlier this year, it put its Copilot teams for consumers and businesses under Jacob Andreou, now its executive vice president of Copilot. Last month, it released a new version of the app with tools for coding and long-running tasks.

Where Copilot is headed: Windows Hybrid Intelligence gives Copilot three new capabilities, as Andreou described them on stage. The assistant can draw on all the files on a PC, take actions such as moving files and changing settings, and hand tasks to AI models running on the machine “when cost or privacy matter more.”
Copilot will still use the cloud for the hardest tasks, Andreou said, and will act on the PC only with the user’s permission.
Microsoft said the features are expected to begin rolling out in the coming months on Copilot+ PCs, the AI-focused Windows machines it introduced in 2024 .

Developers will get a version first. An experimental release coming later this month will let GitHub Copilot automatically send simpler coding tasks to an AI model on the PC and harder ones to the cloud.

In one example depicted on stage, Copilot’s Autopilot agent found an email from Andreou’s accountant, gathered tax documents scattered across his PC, renamed and sorted them into folders, bundled them into a zip file and drafted a reply with it attached, pausing for his approval before sending. The sorting was handled by AI models on the laptop, he said, so the tax details weren’t sent to the cloud.

Running AI models on the PC reduces the usage charges that come with AI in the cloud. Nadella wrote on X that Microsoft is bringing “unmetered intelligence to every desk and every home,” echoing the company’s original mission of “a computer on every desk and in every home.” A slide in the presentation said local models would run tasks on the PC “at no extra cost.”

Microsoft is also adding thousands of quick actions to the search box on the Windows 11 taskbar, such as switching to dark mode, arranging windows or sending a text message. Those start rolling out Wednesday to people in the Windows Insider testing program.
An option to get Copilot answers in the search box will be opt-in and will arrive in select markets later this year, according to the company.

The Recall precedent: Microsoft has run into trouble before with AI that looks at what’s on a PC. Recall, a feature that takes periodic screenshots of a user’s activity to make it searchable, drew objections from security researchers when it was announced in 2024. Microsoft delayed it and made it opt-in before releasing it widely in 2025.
Recall didn’t come up at Wednesday’s event. Microsoft’s blog post says Copilot’s access to local content, which it describes as “files and recent activity,” will require the user’s permission.

Limits on AI agents: Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Windows and Devices, said the AI agents that run on PCs today are “fundamentally insecure because they have broad system access.”

Microsoft’s answer is a technology called Microsoft Execution Containers, now generally available in Windows 11, which lets an organization set which files and networks an AI agent can reach. Microsoft said OpenAI’s Codex and OpenClaw already support it, and that Anthropic’s Claude Code and Perplexity plan to.
Meta’s Muse agent is coming to Windows as an app that uses the technology, as well.
The new PCs: The machines are built around Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip and aimed at developers and creative professionals who want to run large AI models on their own computers.

Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch laptop with up to 128GB of memory, starts at $2,599 and will be available Oct. 16, the same day similar laptops from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo and MSI begin shipping.
A desktop version for developers, the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, costs $5,999 and ships in the U.S. in November.

Microsoft is pitching the laptops against Apple. It says machines with the Nvidia chip start producing AI responses up to 2.1 times faster than a 16-inch MacBook Pro with Apple’s M5 Pro chip and generate AI images up to 4.3 times faster, citing tests it commissioned or that Nvidia ran on preproduction machines.
The company is also offering up to $1,000 back to buyers who trade in a MacBook Pro.
Huang said the chip took more than 4,000 engineering years and started with a conversation he had with Nadella four years ago.

Nvidia’s Windows roots: Sriram Krishnan, the venture capitalist and former White House AI advisor who moderated the conversation, asked Huang for a favorite memory of working with Microsoft. Huang said Nvidia owes its existence to Windows.

He recalled a moment in late 1992, when Windows 3.1 was new and he and his co-founders, who had worked mostly on workstations, started imagining a PC with 3D graphics that could run games and design software. They started the company the next year.
“If not for Windows, Nvidia wouldn’t have been founded,” Huang said.

He traced a line from there to the AI boom. Windows brought graphics chips to the PC, he said, which led to Nvidia’s GeForce chips and its CUDA software, which gave AI researchers the computers they needed for deep learning.
Nadella joked that Huang was “now going to do a little transfer of market cap back to me.” Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company, at about $5.8 trillion. Microsoft is worth about $3.9 trillion.
“Windows has been with me for 34 years,” Huang said at the end of the conversation. “Looks like it’s going to be with me for 34 more.”
“There you go,” Nadella added before they walked off the stage.

articles.title: In effort to diversify economy and build resilience, Seattle Mayor names 18 leaders to new task force
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson is bringing together leaders from Amazon, Spotify, the Port of Seattle, organized labor, technology, cleantech, small business and other sectors as part of a new task force focused on rebuilding and diversifying the city’s economy.

Wilson on Wednesday announced 18 members of the Resilient Seattle Economy Task Force, which will look for ways to remove barriers to business growth, attract and retain companies and improve the process of starting and operating a business in Seattle.

“I’m charging this task force with identifying where the City can make connections, remove barriers and provide support within individual industries and across our economy,” Wilson said. “We need to diversify our economy while expanding opportunities for local entrepreneurs and young people.”

The effort builds on the city’s recently released Seawall: Building a Resilient Seattle Economy report, which called for Seattle to diversify beyond its heavy reliance on large technology companies and focus on sectors including artificial intelligence, cleantech, maritime, life sciences and space.
That report found that companies with at least 100 employees accounted for 74.5% of net job growth in the Seattle metro area from 2014 to 2023, while mid-sized companies accounted for just 16.6%.

The economic challenges have also put a spotlight on Seattle’s tax structure. As GeekWire recently reported, Seattle lost roughly 24,000 jobs between March 2020 and March 2025 even as city tax collections continued to grow, shifting more of the tax burden onto businesses .
Wilson has responded in part by freezing JumpStart tax rates in her proposed 2027 budget, citing “seismic shifts” in the technology sector.

The new task force will initially focus on downtown revitalization, business attraction and retention, cross-sector collaboration, and making it easier to open and operate a business. The task force also comes as Seattle’s business community has pressed City Hall for action on public safety, with dozens of regional CEOs recently calling for a 100-day plan with measurable goals and progress reports.
“Seattle is open for business,” said Beto Yarce, director of the Seattle Office of Economic Development.

articles.title: Opinion: Washington’s new state income tax must be repealed
articles.author: Matt McIlwain
paras: Editor’s note: GeekWire publishes guest opinions to highlight a range of perspectives on issues shaping the tech and startup community. To submit a guest column, email tips@geekwire.com .
This fall, Washington state voters will once again have to defend their economic future and core competitive edge by voting yes on Initiative 645 to repeal the state income tax.

Earlier this year, state lawmakers established the new state income tax. Supporters claim that this tax will only impact higher-income earners. But the measure includes broad new income taxing powers that make every Washingtonian and those doing business in the state a target.
How do we know this? Legislators have made it clear by their actions — and actions speak louder than words!

Most notably, the income tax was written specifically to cover pensions, reversing Washington’s previous commitment to not tax pension retirement income. While teacher, firefighter and other pensioners are not initially paying the state income tax, the only reason to make their income subject to the tax is to require them to pay when it is lowered to apply to them.
Second, Olympia actually voted twice on the income tax — once to pass the income tax, and a second time to ensure they could expand it to everyone. They wanted to make clear their intent to voters.

Finally, the income tax is already driving people out of the state, which will result in lower tax revenues. We can be confident that Sen. Jamie Pedersen (who has stated publicly that he supports a universal income tax on all Washingtonians ) and the Legislature will use that shortfall as justification to apply the tax to many more Washingtonians. So, unless you vote yes on I-645, you can expect to pay the income tax soon.

Even the state’s most prominent Democrats are calling out Olympia’s runaway spending. Former Gov. Christine Gregoire told Washington business leaders recently that Olympia has “a spending problem, not a revenue problem,” noting the state budget has grown from $33 billion to $80 billion since she left office. Former Gov. Gary Locke, similarly, called Olympia’s spending “out of control.”

Two Democratic governors, sounding the same alarm, should tell legislators to focus on spending cuts, not tax increases. But, instead of looking for savings, Washington’s political leaders passed the largest tax and spending increase ($9.3 billion) in state history in 2025, and then followed it up with another $2.3 billion spending increase in 2026.

The pattern is as clear in Washington as it is in other states that are falling behind competitively: no matter how much citizens hand over in taxes, legislators always think it’s never enough. Giving lawmakers even more of our tax dollars when they have failed to responsibly manage what they have hurts everyone in the state.
Beyond the impact to personal paychecks, there are two long-term consequences that will negatively impact voters — whether they pay the tax or not.

First, job creators and job opportunities are leaving the state. National IRS migration data already shows high earners leaving high-tax states at an accelerating rate. Washington ranks sixth highest in the nation for losing higher-income residents, and a state income tax will accelerate this trend. A 2026 Association of Washington Business survey found nearly 1 in 4 Washington employers are now considering relocating out of state, nearly triple the rate from just a year earlier.

Companies such as Starbucks, moving a large share of its corporate workforce to Nashville, are shifting operations and jobs out of the state in response to the increasingly hostile tax climate and the costs of doing business. Sadly, the result is that Washington has an unemployment rate hovering near 5%, tied for sixth highest in the country and nearly a full percentage point above the national average.

Second, avoiding the tax effectively means cutting all ties to Washington. Under the new law, it appears taxpayers can only shed their Washington domicile by spending 30 days or fewer in the state a year and selling their home. It’s no surprise active home listings are up an average 27% in much of Washington this year.

This rule is also an existential threat for the state’s largest nonprofits, as financial advisors are already telling clients the “gold standard” for anyone trying to sever ties is to stop philanthropic giving in Washington entirely.

The last time Washingtonians voted on an income tax was in 2010. That income tax proposal, I-1098, was rejected by a 64%-36% voting margin . Companies including Microsoft, Boeing and Expedia, as well as the founders of Amazon and T-Mobile, supported the effort to stop the income tax. They were right to do so for the benefit of their employees and the citizens of Washington.

In the years since, economic growth and investment enabled the state spending budget to dramatically increase from under $30 billion to more than $80 billion without an income tax. Washington cannot afford to follow the path of states like New York and Oregon, where out-of-control spending leads to higher taxes and an increasingly difficult climate for families and businesses. We need a state that can compete!

This November, voters have the opportunity to send a message to politicians by doing what they have done time and again: vote yes on I-645 to repeal the state income tax and help Washington succeed for generations to come.

articles.title: Sen. Maria Cantwell outlines six-point plan to regulate frontier AI as concerns escalate
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: With President Donald Trump, states and tech giants taking varied and largely uncoordinated steps to put guardrails on artificial intelligence as the technology speeds ahead, U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., has outlined a comprehensive AI governance framework.

“To manage risks from advanced AI systems we need clear safety standards, continuous testing, and reporting of serious failures,” Cantwell said in a statement. “America can lead the world in AI by building systems that are not only more capable, but safer and more secure.”

Last month, Cantwell took to the Senate floor to demand urgent federal regulations and mandatory independent safety testing for frontier AI models before their release. She warned that recent incidents in which autonomous AI agents carried out unauthorized cyberattacks show that dangerous threats are already here, well before the arrival of superintelligence.
The framework proposed Wednesday includes six principles for regulating frontier AI development and deployment:

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith weighed in on the proposal, telling The Seattle Times that the framework “advances the public discussion the nation needs as we consider the future of AI.”

Cantwell, the ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, has a background in technology as a former RealNetworks vice president. She has long pushed for AI regulation, going back to December 2017, when she joined other lawmakers in introducing the bipartisan Future of AI Act.

Two years ago, Cantwell advocated for five bipartisan AI measures included in a larger package of artificial intelligence legislation that addressed many of the concerns outlined in her six principles. Senate Republicans defeated the legislation. Cantwell reintroduced one of the five measures, the Future of AI Innovation Act, in February.

On Sept. 9, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 813 and Assembly Bill 1405, establishing the first state framework for independent assessment and verification of AI safety and risks. On the same day, OpenAI called for mandatory, “capability-based” national regulation — meaning requirements tied to what an AI system can do.

On Sept. 29, Trump announced a voluntary safety agreement with Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google calling for “robust internal controls” to prevent unauthorized hacking and to work with independent external auditors. The deal does not include consequences for noncompliance.

articles.title: Walmart prepares to take off in Amazon’s backyard with Seattle-area drone delivery in 2027
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Walmart looks like it might beat Amazon to the skies over the Seattle area as the retail giant announced this week that it plans to bring automated drone delivery to the region in 2027.

The move is part of a broader nationwide push by Walmart and drone operator Wing — a subsidiary of Google parent Alphabet — to scale across nearly 20 U.S. metropolitan areas. By adding Seattle and Denver in its latest expansion push, the partnership aims to eventually offer 30-minute aerial delivery from more than 270 Walmart stores coast-to-coast, reaching over 40 million potential customers.

Details on which Seattle-area stores will offer the service have not yet been announced. There are no Walmart stores within Seattle city limits, but The Seattle Times reported that permit filings point to initial groundwork underway at store locations in Federal Way and Tacoma.
Federal Way Mayor Jim Ferrell said his community south of Seattle is looking forward to bringing the region “an incredible new convenience” with the advanced delivery solutions.
“The future has arrived and its being delivered by Walmart by drone!” Ferrell said in a news release.

Wing’s electric aircraft fly at speeds up to 60 mph, serving homes within a six-mile radius of participating stores. The drones carry payloads up to five pounds to drop household essentials from groceries to small electronics. Once operational, eligible local shoppers using either the Walmart or Wing app will automatically see airborne drops as a checkout option.
KIRO 7 captured a demonstration of Wing’s delivery system in Bellevue this week, showcasing how the aircraft take off and raise and lower orders.

While Seattle-based Amazon has pushed aggressively to expand its Prime Air drone fleet to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns, the tech giant has yet to launch commercial drone deliveries in its hometown. Instead, Prime Air operations remain concentrated in markets like Arizona, Texas, and Florida.

Amazon isn’t ignoring the Pacific Northwest entirely, however. The Portland Business Journal reported last month that Amazon filed permit applications to build a Prime Air hub at a North Portland facility, targeting an early 2027 launch that has already drawn early pushback from nearby residents concerned about noise and safety.

Those noise concerns mirror a broader backlash taking shape in established test markets. The New York Times and others reported last month on residents living beneath Amazon’s drone flight paths in Richardson, Texas, who have taken exception to the constant low-altitude buzz of delivery aircraft disrupting their suburban way of life.

Wing has sought to head off potential noise backlash by re-engineering its aircraft acoustic profile. According to the company, its latest drones feature custom propellers designed to reduce high-pitched whines, keeping sound levels at roughly 43 to 50 decibels at cruising altitude and around 62 decibels during hovering drops — a level Wing claims is quieter than a standard delivery truck.

But Walmart and Wing have still encountered friction at the local level. In metro Atlanta, county leaders shut down a proposed Walmart drone hub after more than 1,000 nearby residents signed a petition citing noise, safety, and privacy concerns.

articles.title: Ring’s first smart lock ditches the key and adds a dial to revive a dead battery
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Ring is moving from the doorbell to the deadbolt.
The Amazon-owned company on Wednesday announced its first smart lock , a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, said the dial solves the problem that has kept smart locks from catching on the way video doorbells have: when the battery dies, the owner can be locked out. That’s why many smart locks still come with a key.
“If you have to have a key, it’s like, well, why have a smart lock?” Siminoff said in an interview before the announcement.

Twisting the dial somewhere around five to 10 times (depending on how far and how fast it’s turned), generates enough power to turn the lock back on. The light turns green when it’s ready, and the owner can then get in with a fingerprint, the keypad or the Ring app.
Other smart locks offer backups such as terminals for a 9-volt battery or a USB-C port. Those don’t help someone standing at the door at 1 a.m. without a battery or a cable, Siminoff pointed out.

The Ring Smart Lock is due to ship in the first quarter of next year. It runs on a standard Ring battery pack that should last about a year, Siminoff said, and none of its features requires a subscription.
It connects through Amazon Sidewalk, a shared network powered by nearby Amazon devices, and works with Alexa for voice commands and connections to other smart home devices.

The landscape: Ring is entering a market that includes established lock makers such as Schlage, Yale and Aqara. Apple is also preparing its own smart home push, which will include a smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell and security cameras developed with LG Electronics and sold under the LG brand, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

Apple plans to introduce its own smart home devices Oct. 13, and the LG products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months, according to the report. The LG lock supports ultra-wideband, a technology that lets a door unlock automatically as its owner approaches, Bloomberg reported.

Why Ring waited: Siminoff’s first video doorbell, the Doorbot, went on sale in 2013 in a bundle with a smart lock from another company, he said. Ring has since integrated its products with other companies’ locks.
Ring could have put its name on a lock and sold plenty of them, Siminoff said, but he didn’t think the company belonged in the business until it had something different to offer.

The parts inside the new lock are mostly off the shelf, he said, including the components that generate power. The invention was putting them together, and Siminoff said he’s annoyed with himself for not doing it years ago.
“I literally can’t believe that I just didn’t look at this and just fix the damn thing,” he said.

Siminoff, who returned to lead Ring last year, said he worked out the idea on his own computer at night using Amazon’s AI tools, estimating the number of cranks, the cost and whether the parts would fit before handing it to Ring’s engineers. A few years ago, he said, answering those questions would have taken five to 10 engineers and six months.

Privacy and the front door: The lock arrives after a difficult stretch for Ring on privacy. A Super Bowl ad in February for Search Party, a feature that uses AI to scan footage from neighbors’ outdoor cameras for lost dogs, drew a backlash from critics who asked what would stop the same technology from being used to find people.

Days later, Ring canceled a planned partnership with Flock Safety, the license-plate-recognition company, that would have let police using Flock’s platform request video from Ring users. Ring said at the time that the integration never launched and no customer videos were shared.

Asked what he would say to customers wary of giving Ring control of the door itself, Siminoff pointed to Throw Away the Key Encryption, or TAKE, which Ring started rolling out in September and says will become its default. Ring deletes its copies of the encryption keys, the digital codes needed to view customers’ videos, after using them, leaving the keys on customers’ own devices.
“You do not need to compromise on privacy in order to have security,” he said.

At launch, the lock and Ring’s cameras will work together in limited ways. The lock’s activity will show up in the Ring app alongside the company’s doorbells, cameras and alarms, and an owner who sees a visitor on a doorbell camera can unlock the door from the app.

The lock won’t open on its own when a Ring camera recognizes a face. Siminoff said deeper connections between the lock and the cameras haven’t been built, and Ring wants to take the time to get them right.
The lock has no camera of its own. “I think the lock should be a lock and should stay a lock,” he said.

He was also cautious about Amazon delivery drivers using the lock to leave packages inside. Garage delivery is a growing business for the company, he said, calling the garage “the airlock,” a semi-public space between the outside world and the fully private house.
“I still don’t see a world at scale where people are entering homes without the homeowner there,” he said. “It’s not a technology thing. It’s a human thing.”

Ring will expand to other types of locks and other countries if the deadbolt sells, Siminoff said, and tie the lock more closely to its doorbells. He said he’d take on other parts of the door, even the hinge, if he found a way to improve them.
“I never thought we’d do a lock,” he said. “I really didn’t.”

New cameras: Ring also announced five new cameras. Four add to its 4K lineup: the Outdoor Cam 4K Plus ($149.99), Spotlight Cam 4K Plus ($199.99), Floodlight Cam 4K Plus ($219.99) and Indoor Cam 4K ($99.99), the first indoor model in the line. The fifth, the $69.99 Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K , rotates 360 degrees to follow motion.
The two indoor cameras go on sale Wednesday in the U.S., and the three outdoor models are available for preorder.

articles.title: As downtown crime dropped, Capitol Hill may have absorbed the spillover — 2026 trends show signs of relief
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: ALL CRIME TYPES ACROSS CAPITOL HILL, CD, AND FIRST HILL, 2026 AND 2021
From the Seattle Times report on downtown crime displacement

A recent Seattle Times investigation revealed a painful truth in Seattle’s public safety recovery. While aggressive revitalization and targeted enforcement pushed reported offenses in the downtown core down nearly 50% between 2018 and 2025, crime appeared to displace eastward into neighborhoods including Capitol Hill like a “water bed.”

The Times shows that Capitol Hill absorbed the city’s steepest offense spike, while First Hill also climbed. But fresh 2026 data from the Seattle Police Department’s Records Management System illustrates a divergence for the East Precinct with five-year totals showing cooling even as 2026 monthly trends point to a volatile reset under new leadership at the department and City Hall .

In its analysis of Seattle Police Department neighborhood-level data from 2018 through 2025, the Times identified Capitol Hill as the primary recipient of apparent crime displacement radiating outward from increased public safety efforts in downtown Seattle.

While targeted enforcement and public investments drove reported offenses down by nearly 50% in the downtown core, the Times shows Capitol Hill recorded the largest increase in criminal offenses of any neighborhood in the city, adding 780 violent and property crimes over that stretch. By 2025, the neighborhood surpassed downtown to record the highest raw volume of both violent and property offenses in Seattle.

The report shows that these neighborhood-wide increases were not distributed evenly, often clustering in pockets. An SPD analysis cited by the Times showed that from 2024 to 2025, the surge in offenses on Capitol Hill was heavily concentrated within a one-kilometer square area bordering I-5 rather than only along Broadway or Pike/Pine.

The Times also talked with computational social scientist and Capitol Hill Community Council vice chair Curtis Atkisson about how post-pandemic shifts in where people live, work, and spend time altered neighborhood dynamics and fostered patterns consistent with displacement.
CHS looked at the most recent numbers available via the SPD Crime Dashboard .

Comparing 2021 to 2026, the shift out of downtown may be lightening. Overall crime across Capitol Hill, the Central District, and First Hill dropped substantially in the period, driven by broad declines in property crime.

The Central District experienced the sharpest retreat, with total offenses plummeting 44.6% from 1,242 to 688. Burglary dropped 51.2% (213 to 104), larceny-theft fell 47.1% (717 to 379), and robberies halved from 59 to 30. First Hill similarly tracked downward, logging a 21.7% drop from 1,496 to 1,172 offenses, aided by burglaries falling 38.0% (411 to 255) and robberies sliding from 56 to 40.

On Capitol Hill — singled out by the Times as logging the city’s highest offense volume by 2025 — overall crime dropped 19.4% (2,716 to 2,188) in the 2026 vs 2021 comparison. Burglary tumbled 38.4% (734 to 452) and larceny-theft fell 13.5% (1,320 to 1,142). However, violent crime proved stickier: while robbery dropped 20.6% and aggravated assault fell 11.0%, reported rapes jumped 50% from 24 to 36.

The monthly trends across 2026 for the three key neighborhoods may show what is coming next as across the first eight months of complete data in the system, 2026 ran hotter than 2021. Total crime rose from 3,269 January–August offenses in 2021 to 3,623 in 2026 (+10.8%), driven by a 20.3% spike in violent crime that peaked in June at 94 offenses (versus 64 in June 2021). Property offenses mirrored this early climb before flattening around 370–400 monthly reports.

The turning point surfaced midsummer. While 2021 trend lines climbed steadily through the summer, 2026 plateaued and converged. By July (454 vs. 458) and August (463 vs. 466), 2026 overall volume slipped below 2021 baselines, while violent crime fell back to 77 incidents. Rather than endless displacement radiating from downtown, the East Precinct closed the summer on a downward arc.

Overall, the data could represent hope for change. The multi-year record outlined by the Times makes the case that focused enforcement in the urban core inadvertently pushed disorder up the Hill, leaving the area to absorb a bulk of citywide offense increases through 2025. But the cooling seen in five-year comparisons and the midsummer leveling of 2026 suggest this wave may have finally stalled . While the first half of the year brought a jump in monthly offenses, the late-summer retreat below 2021 totals offers some hope that the neighborhood’s crime totals are beginning to bend back downward.

Holding onto that progress, however, is work. As the Times report showed, public safety interventions trickle into adjacent blocks and transit hubs. For neighbors looking to steer that outcome rather than just watch the numbers fluctuate, the Capitol Hill Community Council meets regularly. You can learn more at capitolhillcommunitycouncil.com .

articles.title: Analog Coffee appears ready to break its one-shop rule
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Born 15 years ago on Summit Ave, Capitol Hill’s Analog Coffee is expanding with an ambitious new location on the shores of Lake Union that will have the tiny coffee provider filling a space left empty by Seattle’s coffee giant.

City signage permits reveal the coffee shop is preparing to open in the former Starbucks along Westlake Ave N. The cafe is part of the AGC Building and Marina that rises above the water on the westside of the lake.
The shuttered Starbucks previously occupied a ground-level, drive-through-capable space adjacent to the 10-story office tower.
Fueling drivers would be an interesting shift for Analog.
CHS reported here in 2021 on the cafe’s first ten years on Summit Ave. Founders Danny Hanlon and Tim Hayden once vowed that the original cafe was the only coffee shop they’d ever open. Times change.

Meanwhile, a steady drip of new ventures continues to fill retail spaces left behind by Starbucks continuing to reduce its nationwide retail footprint including stores in its Seattle hometown. While many of what comes next for the spaces is caffeinated like Analog, others like this project in Eastlake represent a new direction for the spaces.
Analog has yet to widely announce the new Westlake expansion and there’s no word, yet, of an opening date but the signage permit has been issued.
In the meantime, you can visit the original at 235 Summit Ave E. Learn more at analogcoffee.com .

articles.title: Seattle City Attorney adds prosecutor roles to target sex trafficking and guns
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans has announced two “historic” prosecutor positions to combat sex trafficking and gun violence.
The Seattle City Attorney’s Office, which traditionally handles only misdemeanors, is expanding its reach into felony-level enforcement through collaboration with the county.

One newly created prosecutor position will be cross-deputized with the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office. The setup allows the attorney to pursue both misdemeanor and felony charges, significantly boosting local capacity to prosecute pimps, sex traffickers, and child exploiters along the Aurora corridor, Evans said.

The second role will lead SCAO’s new Firearms Unit, focusing on Extreme Risk Protection Orders. Working with the Seattle Police Department , this civil prosecutor will facilitate court orders to disarm individuals posing imminent threats of harm.
Mayor Katie Wilson included funding for both roles in her city budget proposal.

articles.title: King County Council approves sales tax increase for family homeless shelters
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The King County Council approved a 0.01% sales tax increase in a 6–3 vote Tuesday to fund emergency shelter and services for homeless children and families. The measure adds one penny per $100 purchase and is expected to raise up to $10 million per year over the next three years.
Taking effect January 1, the hike will push Seattle’s total sales tax rate to 10.56%.

Enabled by recent state legislation, the council was able to enact the tax without a public ballot measure. The statute grants local governments the authority to fund childcare, housing, and youth programs, leaving County Executive Girmay Zahilay discretion to allocate proceeds during upcoming budget cycles.
If individual cities within the county decide to enact their own version of the tax, their collections will offset the county’s share to prevent double taxation.

The increase comes as voters prepare to weigh in on the November ballot including a vote on the 2026 Seattle Transit Measure , a proposed 10-year renewal funded by a 0.3% sales tax championed by Mayor Katie Wilson to allow the city to purchase increased bus service on key routes.
The General Election is Tuesday, November 3rd.

articles.title: Recent SPD Surveillance Audits Highlight Overreach, Vulnerabilities
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Last week, two newly released reports highlighted the vulnerabilities and sloppy implementation surrounding the Seattle Police Department’s (SPD) real-time crime center. Issues discovered included unauthorized Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) cameras being streamed through the center, federal access to SDOT camera data, and a lack of requirements and safeguards for private cameras incorporated into SPD’s system.

The two reports – one from the Seattle Office of the Auditor and the other from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) – come ahead of the anticipated data governance and privacy audit of SPD’s surveillance program conducted by New York University’s Policing Project.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson initiated the Policing Project audit in March amidst privacy concerns around SPD’s surveillance cameras. Wilson paused much of a planned expansion of SPD’s surveillance apparatus while waiting for the audit findings. While cameras weren’t installed in Capitol Hill and the Central District, the new cameras for the Stadium District were installed and turned on for a short time during Seattle’s World Cup games this summer.

In September 2025, the city council voted 7-2 to expand surveillance cameras to the above areas and add SDOT’s traffic management cameras to the real-time crime center. Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Dan Strauss were the two ‘no’ votes.
SPD’s cameras remain operational in the downtown 3rd Avenue core, Aurora Avenue North, and the Chinatown-International District, where there are approximately 308 cameras in 62 different locations.

In addition to those 308 cameras, Hardpressed News reported on an SPD camera on the roof of 12th Avenue Arts in Capitol Hill, and Stop Surveillance City, a local activist group, reported on an alleged camera installation (including 5 cameras) attached to the East Precinct.
The Policing Project audit was expected by the end of September but has been delayed. The Mayor’s Office did not respond to a request for clarification on the expected timeline.
The Policing Project has a stated interest in regulating policing technology rather than outright banning it, a policy preference likely to be reflected in the final audit.

But the two new City reports call into question the implementation of the surveillance program, including a lack of critical agreements, policies, and privacy safeguards put in place, particularly in regard to the SDOT traffic cameras and private cameras being integrated into the real-time crime center.

“These reports underscore the need for meaningful protections and safeguards around law enforcement use of CCTV cameras and real-time crime center software,” said Tee Sannon, the ACLU of Washington's technology policy program director. “These technologies do not reduce violent crime or make our communities safer; they only open more of us to being tracked, especially when police access data from other agencies and privately owned cameras.”

The auditor’s report, released more than a year after the city council voted to incorporate SDOT traffic cameras into SPD’s crime center, revealed that additional unauthorized SDOT cameras not on the public SDOT map have been streaming into the real-time crime center.

“According to SDOT, these cameras were unintentionally included when SDOT provided the list to SPD,” the report said. “SDOT said that it is currently working to remove those camera streams from the Real-Time Crime Center.”
Without the audit, it’s not clear that SPD or SDOT would have addressed these unauthorized camera streams, which still appear to be active for the time being.

The SDOT camera’s surveillance impact report specifically calls out that the cameras “not be used for civil or criminal enforcement purposes.” City staff told the Auditor’s Office that this did not “necessarily” need to be changed since the council passed the real-time crime center bill that allowed the integration of SDOT cameras more recently.

SDOT has not updated its operating procedures regarding how to work with the real-time crime center, including how to communicate when SPD wants a camera to be moved or zoomed and policy for informing SPD about new eligible cameras.

The audit looked into recordings created by SPD of SDOT camera footage over the last year and found that “the Real-Time Crime Center’s practices appear to result in more recordings being created from traffic cameras as compared with SDOT’s practice of manually creating recordings.” More recordings leads to more data that needs to be safeguarded.

But perhaps the biggest finding from the audit was the revelation that the federal government has access to the data from some of SDOT’s cameras. This possibility, and the erosion of civil rights it represents, has been one of the chief criticisms against using surveillance technology in Seattle.

The audit found that SDOT has a contract with the Artificial Intelligence vendor Derq, which says that while the City owns the camera data, for any work that uses federal funds, the federal government has the right to obtain the data, as well as authorize others to receive it. SDOT has used two federal grants on projects using Derq technology, meaning that the federal government is legally able to attain any related data and use or share it as it sees fit, including to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Once an entity has possession of data, they can use any software they choose on that data, including facial recognition software and license plate reading software. The software may be more or less effective depending on the resolution of the available camera data, but the City of Seattle’s prohibition on the use of facial recognition wouldn’t be able to prevent this practice once other entities access the footage.

Finally, the audit said that SPD using the traffic cameras “introduces additional civil liberties considerations and impacts,” pointing out that decisions SDOT now makes about placement of their traffic cameras have more possible unintended consequences. Any decision SDOT makes about where to put a new traffic camera also impacts law enforcement activity in the vicinity, including potential exacerbation of over-policing in poorer and more diverse neighborhoods.

“The fact that SDOT cameras have been regularly accessed by SPD, including via previously undisclosed feeds into the RTCC "by accident," when SDOT's public policy uses literally prohibitive language that those cameras "shall not" be used for policing purposes – this is beyond troubling: it's egregious. Lack of clear additional written policy elsewhere notwithstanding,” WA People’s Privacy wrote to The Urbanist . “WA People's Privacy stands with Community Not Cameras in their call for Seattle to dismantle its dragnet surveillance systems. These systems violate people's first, fourth, and fourteenth amendment rights, and that's a conversation we critically need to have.”

A few days after the audit came out, the OIG released a report on SPD’s surveillance “pilot” that found additional issues, many of which involved SPD’s “Connect Seattle,” which allows people to register their private cameras with SPD or even buy additional hardware that allows their private cameras to stream directly into the real-time crime center.

The Seattle Times reported that 427 cameras are currently streaming into SPD’s real-time crime center, including 23 private cameras. According to public records shared with The Urbanist , at least some of these private cameras are located in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, including at Chophouse Row . 893 additional cameras have been registered with SPD that don’t allow direct access.

The OIG found several issues with the Connect Seattle program. Right now, SPD’s cameras currently in operation are only located in the three original approved zones, but with no formal policy, SPD has opted to allow private cameras to plug into their system from anywhere in the city, which appears to go against the original intent of a limited pilot.

While only public areas are supposed to be surveilled by police cameras, SPD lacks control over private camera orientation and masking, which means abiding by these privacy rules relies on an analyst happening to notice any change that would knock the camera out of scope. Further, the report found that SPD has trouble following the masking requirement for its own cameras with delays observed due to the lack of timely availability of technicians.

SPD also lacks control of data retention times for private cameras. And Communities Not Cameras, a local anti-surveillance coalition, raised a concern about the security of the data provided by those cameras. “Axon supplies the device in every private camera connected to the Real Time Crime Center, and Axon holds federal immigration enforcement contracts. The city cannot yet say what Axon will do with Seattle's data when a federal agency asks for it,” the organization said in a press release.

In addition to the issues around the private camera program, the OIG highlighted that while crime center analysts are prohibited by policy from doing proactive surveillance, there are currently no controls in place to either prevent or monitor this behavior. SPD said they have met with provider Axon to discuss the possibility of adding a search justification requirement in order to view footage, but the real-time crime center has been live since May 20, 2025 without any such safeguards in place.

SPD’s in-vehicle automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), which are also provided by Axon, are currently suspended due to new state-level restrictions imposed by the passage of SB 6002 earlier this year. Before this capability was turned off, the OIG’s report shows that SPD officers were often failing to properly log their searches of this database, a behavior similar to that of law enforcement officers across the country searching Flock data.

“The failure of SPD to even bother to log a rationale for accessing ALPR data 47% of the time in 2025 and inability to limit access by the federal government is equally egregious and points to what we have been saying all along: this is dragnet surveillance, warrantless surveillance, and no private vendor offers the ability to secure the data from the federal government,” the Communities Not Cameras Coalition told The Urbanist .

The new findings from these two reports, which seem to indicate a myriad of problems and a recklessness in implementation on the part of SPD, might make Wilson think twice about resuming the expansion of surveillance cameras across the city. A recent local surge of ICE abductions only highlights the gravity of the possible consequences of her decision.

“Every ICE abduction reinforces the fact that surveillance is dangerous, and that AI-powered mass data surveillance has been downright murderous,” WA People’s Privacy told The Urbanist . “These harms are real and tangible, and mass surveillance is deeply impacting people's lives. This is no longer up for debate.”

articles.title: Mukilteo's Plans for 'Vibrant Waterfront Village' Start to Come Together
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Civic leaders in Mukilteo are advancing a vision for a transformed front porch for their city, work that could turn a collection of vacant, underutilized lots into a "vibrant waterfront village" with public amenities. Despite considerable opposition from Mukilteo residents who would prefer that the city stay focused on turning its waterfront into a public park, this week the Mukilteo Council advanced a zoning change that is intended to unlock a broader range of uses for one of the city's most high-profile areas.

Mukilteo's 1.2-acre "Lot 5" sits just south of the state ferry terminal, a site used by the U.S. Air Force to store jet fuel starting in the 1950s. Following significant remediation work in the 1990s, the Washington Department of Ecology removed Lot 5 from its list of hazardous sites in 2008, and it was ultimately conveyed to the City of Mukilteo in 2016.

Today, the parcel is a gravel lot with just a few picnic tables and some garbage cans, but elected officials in Mukilteo led by Mayor Joe Marine have bigger ambitions for the area. Working with the Port of Everett – which owns several nearby properties including a former NOAA property next door – they are striving to forge a collective vision for a new waterfront district.

In 2022, the Port of Everett hired the architecture and design firm NBBJ to develop a broad, cohesive vision for the full 26-acre waterfront, adopting a vision statement and a set of guiding principles that the City of Mukilteo also signed onto that same year. However, the idea of actually transforming the underutilized parcels hasn't really advanced until this year.

In July, the City issued a request for qualifications (RFQ) seeking a development partner for Lot 5, a move that was called a "first formal step" to achieving longstanding shared goals with the Port around the stretch.

"The envisioned development includes restaurants and cafes with waterfront views, boutique retail, a hotel or inn that puts guests at the edge of Puget Sound, public plazas and gathering spaces, and a continuous promenade along the water’s edge connecting the ferry terminal to Mukilteo Lighthouse Park," a city press release touting the RFQ stated.

Mukilteo did not actually see a stampede of developers looking to get involved with Lot 5, as first reported by the Puget Sound Business Journal , with the RFQ only producing one response. Kirkland-based MainStreet Property Group, which has built nearly 4,000 units across Seattle and the Eastside in recent years, expects to explore a multifamily mixed-use development with below-grade parking, the Journal reported late last month when the RFQ closed.

Though any actual redevelopment proposal remains theoretical at this point, this week the Mukilteo City Council did remove a major impediment that was standing in the way of the city's vision: rezoning Lot 5 from open space to waterfront mixed-use on a 6-1 vote. That vote simply opens the door to broader uses of the parcel, with a potential full conversion to park space still allowed under Mukilteo's zoning if the city decided to change course.

"All you're saying is we're going to rezone that property. Any of those future decisions about leasing the property, what the specific development would look like, those will all still be in the council's hands," Andy Galuska, Mukilteo's Planning and Community Development Director, told councilmembers Monday night. "At no point is the council going to lose control of that process through approval of this rezone. The City still owns the property."
But the rezone still faced considerable community opposition, with a sizable faction of Mukilteo residents wanting the city to commit to maintaining the area as a public park.

"Why can't we just look at open space and water and some green grass and a promenade shore? A walking path, a bike path. Why do we have to muck it up in Mukilteo every time and crap up this beautiful waterfront that we have?" Mukilteo resident Kate Forrester said at a public hearing on the rezone last month. "I want my grandchildren to play down on the beach. You can't have too many parks. That is the only thing that makes a city beautiful. Don't concrete it. Believe me, I came from California, and it's all paved over now."

One major point of contention down the road is likely to be any residential component to a redevelopment proposal. Including housing above amenities built at the ground level is one way that a project on the site could become financially viable, but exactly how many units that would be is sure to be hotly debated in Mukilteo.

Mukilteo has seen tepid housing growth over the last decade, despite ample demand, earning the city a callout as a laggard in a 2023 Urban Institute report by Yonah Freemark analyzing the region's housing deficit. Mukilteo's population has been essentially flat since the 2020 census, according to state estimates that last pegged the city at 21,610 residents.
If the city were to pursuing housing on Lot 5, the issue remains of a covenant tied to the property that restricts residential use altogether.

"There was a condition that residential uses not be located on Lot Five because of the contamination," Galuska said. "So, if any developer or the City in the future wants to develop residential uses there, that would have to be removed. The City Attorney's looked at that provision and thinks that it could be removed if we can prove that site has had some cleanup done on it... if we got that to a level of cleanup where residential is appropriate, that that condition could be could be removed."

The Mukilteo waterfront is a very constrained space, with just one bridge over the railroad tracks for all traffic to get in and out of the area – a bridge that the state highway department is set to replace in the coming years.

The area is fairly well-served by Community Transit buses, but the Sound Transit commuter rail station that provides service to Downtown Seattle is set to be retired in 2033 as Snohomish County's leaders focus on delivering light rail to Everett. Unlike in nearby Edmonds, the city has no Amtrak service, so the sunset of commuter rail would end all train service to that station.

All of which is to say that the topic of parking will be a major issue no matter what ultimately moved forward, but part of the vision for the overall waterfront revamp is creating structured garages under buildings that would allow the sea of stalls surrounding Lighthouse Park to be put to better use. That vision could potentially involve a shuttle bus that serves the waterfront from elsewhere in Mukilteo.
After hearing from members of the public, Councilmember Bob Champion was the sole vote against approving the rezone.

"I kind of think we're jumping the gun. So I can't support changing Lot 5 from open space to mixed use. I think there's plenty of opportunity down the road," Champion said. "I think I counted nine out of every 10 emails I received was, just leave it as open space."
But the majority of the council appears ready to at least open the door to some type of transformation at the city's front door.

"If we choose not to do this today, and we need to go for a rezone later, it's going to put us a year backwards, right? We need to be lockstep with the Port of Everett," Councilmember James Sterba said. "I'm going to keep going back to access to the water. I hear that all the time in all the emails and in the residents that approach me: there will be enhanced access to the water. The plan, as it shows, is every 250 feet off the promenade, there's a way to get to the water. Some of the drawings are spectacular. While while I walk that area myself, it it's not conducive to staying there and hanging out, and really enjoying it because because it's a gravel lot."

Mayor Marine, who has pledged that the city will be a "creative, flexible, and responsive partner" with any developer who is ultimately chosen to advance a plan for the site, framed Monday's vote as a major step.

"This has been a long time in coming," Marine said. "So much time has been spent, and all this really does is moves us to the next level to decide ultimately what we're going to do with that property. It may be a park or it may be development."

articles.title: Rachel Belle eats her way across the Italian Dolomites
articles.author: Rachel Belle
paras: Many years ago, while out on a neighborhood walk, my then-boyfriend asked a question that I imagine he cribbed from his high school guidance counselor, “If you could have any job in the world, and your salary would be a million dollars a year, what would you do for a living?”
My answer was immediate, which surprised me, as I had never thought about this “job” until the words came tumbling out of my mouth.
“I’d like to make sandwiches and deliver them to people hiking in the woods!”

My subconscious delivered the perfect career! I’d get to do the two things I enjoy most: prepare food (don’t worry, I worked at a sandwich shop in college, I’ve got the pedigree for this) and hike! And imagine how stoked people would be to have a really good lunch, that they didn’t have to get up early to make, waiting for them at the top of a mountain!
Rachie’s Summit Subs (Rachie’s Hiking Hoagies??) is still a fantasy, but a few weeks ago I experienced something even better than mountain sandwich delivery: Rifugios in the Italian Dolomites!

Rifugios are high-elevation huts, often found teetering atop mountains, wedged between pointy peaks and nestled into valleys, that appear like a mirage on a hiking trail. They offer lodging for those doing hut-to-hut hikes, but they’re also full-service restaurants, serving hot, tasty, stick-to-your-ribs, house-made dishes, freshly baked cakes and apple strudel, plus a beer and wine list and just as many espresso drinks as you’d find at your favorite cafe.

Imagine being on a 12-mile hike, climbing more than 3,000 feet of elevation, and getting to stop at three rifugios along the way to eat on real plates with actual cutlery and sit outside with gorgeous, unspoiled views sprawled out in front of you. The food isn’t what most would expect in Italy — it’s South Tyrolean; a hearty mashup of Austrian, German, Hungarian and Italian alpine food. Every menu is written in German and Italian and sometimes also in Ladin, the local, preserved language. You'll find spaghetti with tomato sauce, goulash, spätzle, barley soup and gnocchi on the same menu.
Here are some of the meals I enjoyed while hiking the Dolomiti in late September.

Everyone told me I had to try kaiserschmarrn, a fluffy, torn-up dessert pancake that originated in Austria, and luckily it’s on most menus. This one, from Rifugio Vicenza al Sassolungo, had cooked apples and raisins scattered throughout and a loose, homemade lingonberry jam for dipping.

I saw knödel, tender bread dumplings, on every rifugio and restaurant menu I visited in the Dolomiti. These are laced with flecks of speck, salty cured pork found everywhere in the region, served with beef goulash. They’re also commonly served in hot broth.
Most rifugios I visited offered creamy polenta with all kinds of accompaniments, like saucy porcini mushrooms or melted alpine cheese. I chose a well-seasoned, savory sausage.

📍Baite Daniel Hütte This was one of my favorite rifugio meals! Tris di canederli in Italian or knödeltris in German, this trio of bread dumplings are flavored with spinach, beet and cheese, drenched in melted brown butter and topped with freshly grated Parmesan.

📍Almhotel Col Raiser I couldn’t resist this beautiful slice of cake, shingled with juicy Italian plums, lacquered with apricot jam, its crust as dense and tender as shortbread. The freshly whipped cream was dispensed from a large, countertop contraption that I absolutely need to have in my own kitchen. Single use appliances be damned! 📍 Rifugio Friedrich August These coveted, vanilla-cream-filled donuts sell out fast, after having a viral moment on social media, so we made sure to arrive by 8:15 a.m., shortly after they opened. Freshly fried, you can opt for a plop of Nutella or pistachio cream on top; I enjoyed mine with a decaf cappuccino. Rifugio Friedrich August is just a steep 25-minute hike from the parking lot, the first stop on our 12 mile Sassolungo hike.

articles.title: Pop Loser: Ego Death at a Republican Party
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, Hayley Williams has a suggestion for “Nazi bitches,” Kelly Clarkson admitted to being “obsessed” with AI (sigh), Chrissie Hynde shared one of her hottest takes yet, and Justin Timberlake finally apologized for his beatboxing phase. Huge news: I have a new favorite Roxy Music song. Plus, keep reading if you want to see Neil Young “hoover” some pistachios.

This week in Strangerland, instrumental rock trio Bering Sea stopped by the office for another episode of Noise Complaint . Jullianne Bell and I unleashed the first installment of our Scarecrow Psychotronic Movie challenge picks , offering a fucked-up movie recommendation for every day of October (you’re welcome!). Stay tuned for week two, dropping Thursday.

Ego Death at a Republican Party. During her show in California on Saturday, Hayley Williams exclaimed “fuck ICE” and “free motherfucking Palestine” from the stage. Shortly after, a spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security issued a statement to Fox News —because of course they did—stating: “We suggest Ms. Williams to [sic] thank them for their service, not belittle their sacrifice.”
Williams got the last word, posting a screenshot of the DHS statement on her Instagram stories alongside the response : “And may I suggest all Nazi bitches suck on my fat dick.”

Miss AI-dependent. Kelly Clarkson shared some disappointing thoughts about AI on Bowen Yang and Matt Rodgers’ Las Culturistas podcast last week during their recurring “I Don’t Think So Honey” segment, in which host and guest rant about something that makes their blood boil for one minute. Clarkson must have missed the memo on this one, as she launched into a declaration of appreciation, gushing, “I love AI. There are very amazing things with AI that I am obsessed with—and I’m very into it artistically, too.” She declared that her only issue with said technology is when “AI artists” compete on a chart with humans, suggesting they should have their own, separate charts.

Justin Timberlake apologizes for beatboxing, but “can’t promise” it won’t happen again. Timberlake has issued many apologies in recent years, including to the women he’s wronged ( Britney Spears and Janet Jackson ) and for his DWI that “ ruined the tour .” This week, Timberlake took to the comment section of an Instagram video by pop culture historian Hannah Young’s, in which she addressed Timberlake’s history of compulsive beatboxing. He commented, “I often look back on that time as well. I still haven’t come up with any answers. I don’t know how to apologize enough for whatever those ambitions were.” He continued, “I hope you can forgive me. Also, I can’t promise I won’t do it again. God help us all.”

To each one’s own. Chrissie Hynde is no stranger to hot takes, good and bad. In the last year alone, she’s defended Brigitte Bardot’s legacy, compared concertgoers glued to their cell phones to “monkeys wanking,” and stated that she wants nothing to do with the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. This week, she added a plot twist by praising Taylor Swift’s widely disliked new song “Cleveland!” Hynde wrote on her Instagram : “I was thrilled to hear Taylor Swift’s new song, Cleveland. Now there’s a girl who stays on the cutting edge…”

New music incoming! Local legends Chastity Belt have announced their forthcoming album All My Friends , and dropped two tracks for early listening, “I Could Say Less” and “Pavement.” Electropop queen Slayyyter also revealed the name of her upcoming album, wor$t man in america (the “brother” album to her previous album, WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA ) . Meanwhile, Mogwai collaborated with Iggy Pop on their new song “Underground,”and Bonny “Prince” Billy has detailed his upcoming tribute album to the Dutch singer-songwriter Jules de Corte.
Now, take a deep breath and enjoy… Neil Young “hoovering” pistachios at an airport lounge.

This week, I finally watched the 1980 girl band classic, Times Square . The film follows two thirteen-year-old best friends who escape a mental hospital to live in an abandoned warehouse, where they make their own clothes and pursue their creative dreams of poetry and punk rock. The film has a perfect soundtrack of new wave and punk staples (Patti Smith, Gary Numan, Talking Heads, etc.), opening with Roxy Music’s addictive “Same Old Scene.” I can’t stop listening to this song.
“High Heels and Blue Jeans” by Jess Williamson

My personal most-anticipated album of the year, Jess Williamson’s A Mile South of Heaven , is out this Friday, and I couldn’t be more excited. “High Heels and Blue Jeans” is my favorite track she’s released from the album so far—it’s playful yet heartbreaking. articles.title: Slog AM: Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes Now Has a Bullshit Job, Trump Wants Iran to Nuke LA and San Diego, Autumn Is Here
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes will now bring home the bacon by way of the private sector. He joined MissionRT, a company that “advises law-enforcement agencies on leadership, technology, and organizational change.” Why does all of this remind me of that book by the late anarchist and anthropologist David Graeber, Bullshit Jobs, A Theory ? In Graeber’s words: “Provisional Definition 2: a bullshit job is a form of employment that is so completely pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even the employee cannot justify its existence.”

Bruiser, the only elk on Whidbey Island has died. He was beloved by the community, who, according to the Seattle Times , fed him “apples, corn and potatoes” during the 14 years he spent on what must have appeared to him to be pretty much heaven. He didn’t have much to do but go this way and that, and never once attempted to leave the way he arrived on the island: by swimming. The lone elk, a local icon, was famous for his tangled antlers. Earth, receive an honoured guest , Bruiser the bull is laid to rest.

For the next few days, expect what you will experience today: morning mists or fogs, and sunny afternoons. Also, have you seen the trees around town? Autumn is finally here, and the leaves, red and gold, are soon to fall, or are falling, or have fallen. There are few things more beautiful than the sight of summer’s glorious death. In fact, I wish it lasted longer. Lasted until late November. I also wish people who don’t like walking on summer’s demise would use a rake instead of that loud gas guzzling machine. Expect a high of 66.

What’s Trump up to now? During some rally in Nebraska, he recommended that Iran nuke San Diego and Los Angeles . Of course, he has nothing to offer rural voters—who are feeling great pain at the pump and grocery store—but more and more of the same anti-urban and anti-diversity “ psychological wage .” The president, however, failed to mention San Francisco. Why? My guess is from Yahoo Finance : “Nvidia stock rises to new highs as market cap closes in on $6 trillion.” LA just makes movies, and San Diego only has military bases.

What a 21st-century mess this is. The sister of an Arizona road rage victim, Christopher Pelkey, who was shot to death by Gabriel Horcasitas, used an AI video of her brother to ask the judge to go easy on the defendant . In the words of AI Pelkey: “To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me: It is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances… In another life, we probably could have been friends. I believe in forgiveness.” Though the AI Pelkey was “loved” by the judge, he still gave Horcasitas the maximum sentence. But the court was so bewildered by this novel use of AI, that it ultimately threw out the ruling and “[remanded] for resentencing.” Unlike the court in the film Rashomon , which is set in 12th-century Japan, modern US courts have yet to accept testimonies from ghosts (AI or otherwise).

Dr. Paul Allen (yes, there is more than one of them, and some are still alive), a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center suspects that “the botched execution of Christa Pike,” resulted from the executor’s failure to place the needle into a vein. As a consequence the poison only reached “peripheral tissues in the arm.” This apparently explained the “arm throbbing” witnessed by observers.

Now let me tell you something. If you’re going to execute me, you must use electricity or a gun or rope because I, too, have veins that are nearly impossible to find. (If you want my blood, you have to abandon the inside of the elbow and instead go for the wrist, which, for some reason I’ve never understood, is not ideal and even despised by nurses and technicians.) Well, Christa Pike regained consciousnes s yesterday. She is even talking to the living, but sustained “severe damage to her arms.” Her lawyer expects a “long recovery.” Well put. Let her recovery last for as long as she lives. In short, the death penalty must be abolished.

A quick thought. Though the future for Christa Pike is presently unclear (will they or will they not make a second attempt to kill her?), this nearly unprecedented situation has nevertheless entered a metaphysical zone. Meaning, Pike’s predicament is no longer just legal, but now also has a supernatural aspect. This matters because we live in a very superstitious society, and so many will see the failure to execute Pike as nothing less than a sign from the other side. The Old One is clearly saying something to us mere mortals. And do you want to be the one who dismisses a message from the Old One? He clearly said: Let Pike live goddamnit . And, amazingly, she is still here, still in the world. Now, who are you “to go against the wind?”

Let me tell you a great ghost story. It involves a black hole. The question is this: Where does a black hole’s gravity come from? The rough answer: From the ghost of a star. A star that’s no longer around. What happened? During the collapsing process of forming an event horizon, a black hole’s point of no return, time around the star became slower and slower, the greater and greater the collapse. Finally, the dying star’s gravity froze , stopped in time, and became a ghost of gravity because its fallen star no longer communicates with the universe we observe. End of story.

There is a whole movement of philosophical thought —indeed, the dominant movement since Kant—that is convinced that all things require a relation to exist, correlationism, because how can anything, even numbers, exist without an observer. Yet, we know there are places in time and space that exist without relationships or encounters. For example, once, before the explosion of the star whose dust is our sun and before us, there was simply nothing where I am now (in my home office on October 7, 2026), and, if the open universe theory is correct, or if the big crunch theory is correct, there will also be in the future nothing where I am at this moment.

What I find most fascinating about the mind is it can relate with things—a lonely piece of ice drifting through space five billion years ago; the terrific density of a neutron star that is a billion years away from now. And yet, the mind knows these things can never be seen or exist in any sensible way. A big part of our real is wholly impossible.

articles.title: Many drugs have mirror chemical structures, one helpful and the other harmful – a Nobel-winning discovery allows chemists to make either on demand
articles.author:
<name>Sajish Mathew, Associate Professor of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Maryland Eastern Shore</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sajish-mathew-1354741"/>
paras: The effects a drug or chemical compound have on the body depend on how its atoms are arranged in space. Some compounds have a dark twin with the same molecular formula but different 3D structure – and this can have consequences for what they do or don’t do in the body.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry was awarded to two researchers who developed a chemical process allowing them to create only one of these two twins. Called asymmetric organic synthesis , this discovery meant that chemists developing pharmaceuticals could create one version or the other – for example, only the version of the molecule that benefits the body, not the version that can cause damage.

Consider the tragic story of thalidomide , a morning sickness drug that caused thousands of birth defects and miscarriages. While one form , or isomer, of thalidomide has a sedative effect, the other is thought to cause abnormal physiological development. Because the two versions can convert back and forth in the body , it’s dangerous to take either form of thalidomide while pregnant.

My research has focused on one such compound found in red grapes and peanuts: resveratrol. It has been a scientific mystery why clinical trials on using resveratrol to treat Alzheimer’s disease have had inconsistent results. With the help of the chemical reactions that led to the 2026 Nobel Prize, my team and I discovered that it may be because two different forms were used – while one may help with cognition and memory, the other may be toxic to the nervous system.

Many drugs have the same atoms and bonds but are arranged differently in space. These drugs are called chiral compounds – meaning they exist as two nonsuperimposable mirror images. For example, your hands are also nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other. Although they look the same, they don’t overlap when you put one on top of the other.

Usually these mirror-image versions have very similar properties because they share the same elements and bonds. But the way they are arranged in space can drastically change the effects they have in the body. Just as you wouldn’t be able to fit a left-handed glove on your right hand, a left-handed version of a drug wouldn’t be able to fit into a target in the body shaped to fit a right-handed molecule.

Chiral molecules come in two versions, or isomers, defined by their optical activity . This means that if you shine polarized light on a chiral molecule, one will rotate the light to the left (indicated by the prefix L-, or levorotatory) while the other will rotate it to the right (indicated by the prefix D, or dextrorotatory).

Amino acids , the building blocks of proteins, are chiral molecules. Living organisms primarily make proteins from amino acids with L configurations . The D configuration, however, has many other functions in nature. Bacteria , for example, use D configuration amino acids to make their cell walls. Mammals use D configuration amino acids as messengers in their nervous and endocrine systems.

The amino acid tyrosine is one important exception to the L configuration rule. Unlike other amino acids, both the L and D configurations of tyrosine can be activated for protein synthesis by an enzyme called tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase (TyrRS) .

The presence of D-tyrosine can make it difficult for cells to synthesize proteins that only use L-tyrosine. However, cells have evolved enzymes that can discriminate between both versions and ensure that only L-tyrosine is used. When tyrosine-consuming enzymes are absent, the resulting increased levels of tyrosine in the body can have toxic effects , including damage to the nervous system .

Recently published work from my lab suggests a potential reason why too much tyrosine can be neurotoxic. When we added increasing amounts of L-tyrosine to rat brain cells in a petri dish, we found that it decreased levels of TyrRS, the enzyme that activates tyrosine to make proteins without causing damage to the body. Surprisingly, adding D-tyrosine not only caused TyrRS levels to drop, but also killed the neurons.

When we looked at the brains of Alzheimer’s patients who show increased tyrosine levels, we also found that TyrRS enzyme levels are depleted. Our hypothesis is that as tyrosine levels in the brain increase, TyrRS enzyme levels drop and cause damaging effects on the brains of those with Alzheimer’s. These findings indicate the potentially important role TyrRS may play in the synthesis of proteins essential for cognition and memory.

These findings have implications for studies on resveratrol , a compound found in red wine that researchers have been examining for potential health benefits. While some clinical trials found that resveratrol can improve cognitive function in people with Alzheimer’s disease, others found it had the opposite effect and made the disease more severe. Why resveratrol can have such varying effects has remained a scientific enigma.

Resveratrol comes in two forms, cis-resveratrol and trans-resveratrol. The “cis-” and “trans-” prefixes , much like L- and D-, describe how the same atoms in two isomers are arranged differently in space.

My colleagues and I found that because the two forms of resveratrol bind to TyrRS in different ways , they can result in opposite effects in neurons . While cis-resveratrol was able to increase TyrRS levels in rat neurons in a petri dish, high concentrations of trans-resveratrol depleted TyrRS and caused neural damage. However, low concentrations of trans-resveratrol can convert into cis-resveratrol in the body. This result leads to an increase in TyrRS levels and its associated benefits.

We hypothesize that many clinical trials on resveratrol failed because none tested cis-resveratrol alone. We believe that this may also explain why trials that used high doses of trans-resveratrol saw harmful effects, while trials that used low doses of trans-resveratrol that were then converted into cis-resveratrol in the body saw beneficial effects.

Beyond the individual atoms and bonds of molecules, the body also cares about how they’re arranged in space. Paying attention to the different forms a drug takes could help lead to more effective treatments.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Aug. 3, 2022 .
