articles.title: From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication
articles.author:
<name>Seth T. Kannarr, Visiting Honors Lecturer, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/seth-t-kannarr-1390874"/>
paras: Articles published in The Conversation go well beyond academics writing for a general audience – they can also serve as great content for educators to use in the classroom.

Our recent article in the academic journal The Professional Geographer explores how articles from The Conversation provide opportunities for public storytelling and authentic learning in university classrooms.

As geographers and experienced writers for The Conversation – having written or co-written 26 articles since 2017 – we understand firsthand the value of disseminating these short, open-access articles that can be easily republished under the Creative Commons license .
To this point, one of the top republishers for The Conversation is Actively Learn , a McGraw Hill platform used to provide standards-aligned content for K–12 educators.

Yet we feel that The Conversation’s potential contributions to university education have not been sufficiently explored, which is unexpected given that its articles are authored by college teachers and researchers.

Public storytelling is increasingly important for scholars as higher education faces increased scrutiny , politicized attacks on truth-telling , pressure to show broader relevance and calls to regain trust .

In our article, we argue for integrating more public-facing science communication into educational spaces. We also introduce our use of articles from The Conversation as a classroom tool and discuss coaching students through challenges they face.

Our pedagogical work may interest university educators in other fields looking for ways to engage their classrooms in “ authentic learning ” – that is, learning in real-world contexts – and incorporate public storytelling into the professional preparation of their students.

Authentic learning gives students opportunities to observe how subject experts apply academic research to address social, political and environmental issues and contribute to public and policy debates and decisions beyond the classroom.

We choose to use articles from The Conversation in pedagogical exercises because we want to challenge students to confront societal issues from new perspectives. The goal is to do our part as university educators to help produce scholar-citizens ready for civic engagement.

For example, in an end-of-semester writing assignment we have hosted, students were tasked with selecting a pressing issue in the course’s scope and writing a short article in the style of The Conversation.

Students were asked to draft a “pitch” for an article before writing it, just like prospective authors do for The Conversation. They were asked to make revisions, think through how to support their claims with evidence and adapt to the various conventions of writing for the public, similar to how it may go in working with the editorial team.

Although it is a sometimes difficult and often humbling process for the students to go through, they in real time understand the struggle of writing concisely and interestingly for a general audience.
They also produce a well-written short article that they can be proud of and potentially publish in an appropriate outlet or include in a portfolio for a potential employer.

Although The Conversation does not allow undergraduate students or community partners to go through the process of submitting a pitch and drafting an article to be published, our previous students have shown their ability to punch above their weight and produce short articles that demonstrate their applied and rigorous understanding of course concepts.
As scholars, we like to write for The Conversation for four primary reasons:
First, we love the challenge of taking our discipline-specific academic work and translating it into jargon-free, accessible writing that anyone in our family or community could easily read.

This can be a difficult process – especially in taking complex academic concepts and breaking them down into simpler language while keeping essential rigor and nuance. The editors we work with from The Conversation are helpful in this case – even if the process is sometimes maddening along the way.

Second, we love tracking the readership of the published pieces in The Conversation’s dashboard portal. It is exciting to see a recently published article cross a threshold, such as 70,000 reads, over a period of time – something you would never experience from a traditionally published academic journal article.
These aren’t just numbers for us – it’s an indication of the potential impact of our work.

Third, we love how easy it is to share our articles via social media or via DOI links. Additionally, when other news and media outlets republish our pieces via the Creative Commons license, our work gets disseminated widely.
There is no paywall preventing access, no login or account required. Our wider communities can read the short piece by simply clicking a link that can be texted to them.

Fourth, our previous articles published in The Conversation are great sources for assigned reading in our seminar courses. They often cover content that we teach in our courses and are written in our voices. They also are short and easy to read for busy students – while laden with helpful hyperlinks to sources to explore further.

Writing for The Conversation allows us to produce accessible course content that we can use and share for years to come. From our experiences, students who read the articles have enjoyed them as much as we do, because they are quick reads and written in an interesting and accessible manner.
Further research studies could be done to quantitatively measure student learning outcomes when using articles from The Conversation.

Although our published article is helpful in providing anecdotal insights of the results we have seen from our experiences, more research would allow for further ways to measure the impact of using these articles in the classroom.

We believe The Conversation can help higher education even further by having teams or boards of educators working together to assemble college classroom e-books of articles organized around certain themes of instruction. This expansion of academic insights can help our students, who represent future civic decision-makers and public storytellers.

Regardless of future research opportunities, educators can choose to integrate articles from The Conversation into their classrooms now – whether using these articles for assigned content reading or for creative writing exercises.
We have seen firsthand the benefits of doing so, and we encourage more educators to join us. In doing so, your students can join the broader public conversation – with the power of The Conversation.

articles.title: These state supreme court races could decide abortion access and trans rights
articles.author:
<name>Rachel Rebouché, Professor of Law, The University of Texas at Austin</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rachel-rebouche-1389508"/>
paras: In the heated news coverage of what’s at stake in the 2026 midterms , state supreme court races are drawing relatively little attention. Yet these are highly significant elections.
Thirty-one states are holding supreme court elections in 2026, with voters nationwide picking judges to fill more than 60 open seats.

As a law professor whose research and writing focuses on reproductive health , I’m watching these races closely. That’s because in the coming years these courts will have the final word on many consequential legal fights around abortion and trans healthcare.

When the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 , ending a half-century of federal constitutional protection for abortion, it handed this major issue back to the states. As a result, in addition to prompting ballot initiatives, the court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization has also spurred litigation in state courts.
These cases ask judges to discern, for example, whether state constitutions create a right to abortion – or, at least, prohibit restrictions on abortion access .

Moreover, in weighing the legality of abortion bans , state judges must determine specific issues of abortion access. Idaho’s high court recently approved Republican officials’ rewritten wording for a ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s abortion ban; advocates for the initiative argue that the language misrepresents Idaho’s abortion law.

In Indiana, the state Supreme Court recently heard arguments over whether a religious freedom law creates an exception to the state’s near-total abortion ban. The plaintiffs in that case argued that their faiths allowed or required the procedure in circumstances the ban currently forbids.
Increasingly, the U.S. Supreme Court has been handing questions concerning transgender rights back to states, too.

In June 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in United States v. Skrmetti that Tennessee’s ban on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for transgender minors does not count as sex discrimination under the U.S. Constitution. Consequently, that and similar bans only need to pass the lowest level of judicial review; they no longer have to pass the higher bar of “strict scrutiny.”

This means lower courts can essentially rubber-stamp the bans that state legislatures have passed. In fact, the Skrmetti decision cleared the way for the roughly two dozen states with similar bans to keep enforcing them.

Skrmetti did not, however, require any state to pass such a law. And it does not address how far the ruling extends to adults or whether it applies to other related aspects of gender-affirming care, such as insurance coverage.

In other words, the people who now decide whether abortion restrictions stay on the books or whether a minor can get gender-affirming care are, in many cases, not justices sitting on the U.S. Supreme Court. In many cases, they will be state supreme court judges.

In Montana, judicial races could change the ideological bent of the state’s top court. Judicial elections in the state are technically nonpartisan, but Republicans see a chance to retake the state Supreme Court with judges they endorse.

In 2023, its Democrat-endorsed majority ruled that the state constitution protects abortion rights. It also determined that attempts to stop one class of health providers – advanced practice registered nurses – from performing abortions violated those rights.

Judges who upheld restrictions affecting residents’ reproductive rights will face voters this fall in Alabama, Arizona, Florida, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Texas . In some of these races, abortion is a live – and legally dynamic – issue.

North Carolina’s high court also leans heavily conservative. This year one of just two Democrats on the seven-judge panel – incumbent Democrat Anita Earls – is up for reelection. If she loses, the GOP would gain a near-total supermajority on North Carolina’s Supreme Court. That outcome would likely cement the party’s edge on key political matters for years to come.

Michigan looks like the mirror image of North Carolina. All justices there are officially nonpartisan, but Democrat-backed justices hold a 6-1 majority on the seven-member court. Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh and Justice Noah Hood – both Democrats – are up for reelection this fall.

Democrats are hoping to retain their edge, in part to keep abortion protected. Voters enshrined abortion rights directly into Michigan’s Constitution in 2022, and the state’s highest court has already interpreted that amendment to dismiss abortion-related restrictions .

Ohio is a powerful example of what is at stake in this year’s state supreme court races. Republicans hold a 6-1 majority on the state’s high court, a dominant position built over successive election cycles in 2022 and 2024.

In the 2026 midterms, Ohio’s only Democratic state Supreme Court justice, Jennifer Brunner, is defending her seat against a Republican challenger . If Brunner loses, Ohio’s highest court could become a unanimous conservative bench – one that will likely determine the outcome of high-profile cases related to both abortion access and gender-affirming care.

Ohio voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2023 protecting abortion access . The amendment establishes that individuals have the right to make their own reproductive decisions. The language covers contraception, fertility treatment, continuing a pregnancy, miscarriage care and abortion up to fetal viability. It also asserts that the state generally cannot interfere with these decisions.

Now, lower courts are litigating whether restrictions on abortion access – for instance, the state’s 24-hour waiting period and ban on telehealth for medication abortion – can survive scrutiny under that amendment.
The Ohio Supreme Court may eventually decide that case. In my assessment, an even more conservative Ohio court might be inclined to read the voter-approved abortion amendment as narrowly as possible.

Ohio’s Supreme Court is similarly poised to make big decisions on trans rights. For example, it could uphold the state’s ban on gender-affirming care for transgender minors. That would reverse a 2025 appellate ruling that had struck down the law, which was passed over the veto of Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.

Even if they don’t change the partisan makeup of these courts, elections for state supreme court seats in places such as Ohio may matter for the scope and breadth of rulings that claw back individual rights. Or they may foretell how a conservative near-supermajority might lock in abortion and trans restrictions for a generation.
Whoever wins these judicial races in November will not just be interpreting the law. In a real sense, they will be writing the next chapter of it.
This story was produced in collaboration with Rewire News Group , a nonprofit newsroom that covers reproductive health.

articles.title: Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction
articles.author:
<name>Christos Makridis, Associate Research Professor of Information Systems, Arizona State University; Institute for Humane Studies</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christos-makridis-2498826"/>
paras: The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more flexible arrangements , such as hybrid or remote work.

But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that workplace factors like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office.

To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person.
These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers.

As a researcher of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar Jason Schloetzer that analyzed responses from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager.

Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest.
In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy.
Semi- or fully remote workers may appear more satisfied . But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue.

Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately.

A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable.

We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work.

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion.

Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report , 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely.

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience.

Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an American Medical Association survey in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages.
The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession.

Meanwhile, separate Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines.

Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations.
Those problems require attention wherever employees work.
The expression “work-life balance” implies that it’s healthy to engage in social activity with friends and family outside work.

But as other research of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job.

Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them.

Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, according to new research published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst.
These findings raise a practical question for employers: How can time together at work become more useful?

For employers considering a return to the office, a useful starting point is to first identify what employees gain from being together and then organize office time around it. Teams that depend on frequent collaboration need overlapping schedules. Newer employees need access to colleagues who can teach them. Managers need to provide useful feedback and address workload issues wherever people work, and employees need to be responsive to managerial efforts to engage them.

Employee preferences and job requirements differ across organizations, so managers need to determine which arrangements suit their teams. But regular, useful feedback matters across on-site, hybrid and remote settings. That means discussing priorities, recognizing employees’ contributions and helping them work effectively with colleagues.
As Gallup workplace researcher Jim Harter has suggested , this kind of feedback should become a weekly habit.
“These conversations don’t have to be long; 15 to 30 minutes, done consistently, is enough,” he wrote.

articles.title: AI can help with academic research but doesn’t always get it right – here are some tips to check the information you receive
articles.author:
<name>Allison Faix, Librarian and Instruction Coordinator, Coastal Carolina University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/allison-faix-2733639"/>
paras: Almost 25% of adults in the United States are using artificial intelligence chatbots on a daily basis, a 2026 Pew Research Center study found.
At the same time, another recent study found that 48% of the information that popular free chatbots gave in response to questions about the news contained errors .
As librarians , we know that if students are using AI chatbots to help with their academic research, they shouldn’t assume that the information they’re given is accurate.
Not all AI is the same. Here are four steps we recommend to question information AI generates, including by checking the original source and considering issues that aren’t always easy to spot.
First, we think it makes sense to spend time choosing the right AI tool for the task at hand.

AI tools – be it ExLibris’ Primo Research Assistant , Research Solutions’ Scite , Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – are trained with various datasets and use different algorithms to generate results. They should not be used interchangeably.
Some tools might be better or worse at answering specific kinds of questions, and the types of answers they generate can vary.
People might choose ChatGPT , for example, at the beginning of their research process, because it can provide overviews and summaries to help with understanding concepts.
In subsequent stages, they might choose a tool such as Primo Research Assistant or Scopus AI, which can help find and examine peer-reviewed research that has been vetted by academics.

Students conducting academic research could also see whether their library subscribes to an artificial intelligence tool like LeapSpace or Concensus , which draw their data from peer-reviewed, scholarly research.
Using these specific AI tools doesn’t eliminate the need to evaluate their answers, but it provides more certainty that the data has gone through a review process.

Tools such as Anthropic’s Claude, meanwhile, may also draw from academic research, but to what extent is unclear. According to Anthropic, Claude states that it is trained on a proprietary mix of publicly available information from online sources, public and private datasets, user data and synthetic data generated by other models .
Finally, it can be helpful to read librarians’ reviews about AI tools to help select the best fit. People can also take a simple online test such as ROBOT to help them consider which tool to use.
Second, asking follow-up questions is an important part of evaluating the answers AI tools generate. Even if the answer an AI tool gives sounds good, it is useful to take time to learn more about it.

Checking one’s own emotions is also important, because AI chatbots have been known to flatter users by giving answers based on the user’s own biases , or what the user wants to hear , rather than just facts.

Ask the AI to tell you where it got the information, how confident it is that the answer is correct and what might be missing. Ask the AI why it believes the answer is correct, or ask it to explain how it came up with an answer.

It’s helpful to also make sure your prompt is phrased in a neutral way. For example, asking “What does psychological research say about social media and anxiety?” rather than “Tell me why social media causes anxiety” may produce different responses.
Third, it is useful to trace any claims the AI chatbot makes to their original sources.
Students may be familiar with using the SIFT process to evaluate websites. This process asks people to stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to their original source.
Start by asking the chatbot to cite its sources, if it did not do that already.

Then, go to each source and read enough to figure out whether the AI is using the information in the right context. Also, look into who authored the source and whether they have expertise in the topic. If the AI won’t cite the sources it used, or if the sources it cites don’t include the information it said they did, pull out any claims it is making and do further research.

Can you find other, credible sources that back up what the AI is saying, using Google or a library database? Can you figure out where the AI may have gotten the information and whether that source is credible?
If this seems like a lot of work, you could always go directly to library databases instead of using AI tools.
Fourth, there are other, less visible issues that can play out when using AI tools.
For example, it might not always be easy to tell whether an AI tool is missing important perspectives or is giving biased information.

Remember that you, not the AI tool, are the researcher. It might be easy to rely on an AI tool to generate a summary of important sources, but deciding for yourself what sources to use helps you learn about a topic more deeply.

Research shows that most AI tools focus on sources such as websites, internet forums and other online content that is freely available and written in English . Consider what expert knowledge might be missing from AI datasets and seek out those viewpoints when needed.
Last, remember that you need to cite the AI tool you used if you are quoting or paraphrasing text generated by it in your work, just as you would cite any other source.
Artificial intelligence is changing fast. As librarians, we think it is important to continually evaluate whether the tools you are using are still working for you.
These tips are a good place to start to help sharpen your evaluation skills.

articles.title: Armed poll watchers: New Jersey’s 1981 racist voter intimidation campaign is a cautionary tale ahead of 2026 midterms
articles.author:
<name>Mark Krasovic, Associate Professor of History and American Studies, Rutgers University - Newark</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mark-krasovic-1116385"/>
paras: In the history of voter suppression in the United States, including attempts to stop Black and Latino people from voting, Republican tactics in the 1981 New Jersey gubernatorial race stand out.
That November, voters in several cities saw posters at polling places printed in bright red letters: “WARNING. This area is being patrolled by the National Ballot Security Task Force .”
About 200 patrols were deployed statewide, many of them uniformed and carrying guns.

In Trenton, patrol members asked a Black voter for her registration card and turned her away when she didn’t produce it. Latino voters were prevented from voting in Vineland, while in Newark some voters were physically chased from the polls by patrolmen, one of whom warned a poll worker not to stay at her post after dark. Similar scenes played out in at least two other cities, Camden and Atlantic City.
Weeks later, after a recount, Republican Thomas Kean won election as governor by fewer than 1,800 votes.

Democrats, however, soon won a significant victory. With local civil rights activists, they discovered that the “ballot security” operation was a joint project of the state and national Republican committees. They filed suit in December 1981, charging Republicans with “efforts to intimidate, threaten and coerce duly qualified black and Hispanic voters.”

In November 1982, the case was settled when the Republican committees signed a federal consent decree – a court order applicable to activities anywhere in the U.S. – agreeing not to use race in selecting targets for ballot security activities and to refrain from deploying armed poll watchers.
That decree expired in 2018 after Democrats failed to convince a judge to renew it.
The 1981 voter suppression efforts resonate today in the midst of the Trump administration’s persistent efforts to suppress the vote and undermine trust in elections nationwide.
In May 2026, a PBS reporter asked President Donald Trump whether he would send the National Guard or ICE to polling places in the midterm elections.
“ He did not rule it out ,” wrote reporter Liz Landers.

Considered an early referendum on Ronald Reagan’s presidency, New Jersey’s 1981 gubernatorial race featured Kean – with Roger Stone at the campaign’s helm – promising corporate tax cuts and relying heavily on Reagan’s endorsement.
State and national Republican party officials then devised a project they claimed would prevent Democratic cheating at the polls.

In the summer of 1981, the Republican National Committee sent an operative named John A. Kelly to New Jersey to run a ballot security effort. Kelly had previously served as one of the RNC’s liaisons to the Reagan White House .

In August 1981, under the guise of the National Ballot Security Taskforce, Kelly sent about 200,000 letters marked “return to sender” to voters in heavily Black and Latino districts. Those whose letters were returned had their names added to a list of voters to be challenged at the polls on Election Day, a tactic known as voter caging .

In the Newark area, Kelly produced a list of 20,000 voters whom he deemed potentially fraudulent. He then hired local operatives to organize patrols, ostensibly to keep such fraud at bay. To run the Newark operation, he hired Anthony Imperiale .
Imperiale, in turn, hired off-duty police officers and employees of his private business, the Imperiale Security Police, to patrol voting sites in the city.

The gun-toting, barrel-chested former Marine had first adopted the security role during Newark’s 1967 uprising – five days of protests and a deadly occupation of the city by police and the National Guard following the police beating of a Black cab driver. During the uprising, Imperiale organized patrols of his predominantly white neighborhood to keep “ the riots ” out.

Soon, Imperiale became a hero of white backlash politics. His opposition to police reform earned him widespread support from law enforcement. And his fight against Black housing development in Newark’s North Ward delighted many of his neighbors. By the end of the 1970s, Hollywood was making a movie based on his activities.
After serving as an independent in both houses of the state legislature, Imperiale became a Republican in 1979 . Two years later, he campaigned with Kean.

Once in office, the new governor named Imperiale director of a new one-man state Office of Community Safety – an appointment often interpreted as reward for Imperiale’s leadership of the ballot efforts in Newark, but stymied when Democrats refused to fund the position .

Despite Kean’s slim margin of victory, Democrats at the time were careful not to claim that Republican voter suppression efforts had decided the election. In 2016, the former Democratic candidate claimed they did indeed make the difference .

Rather, the state and national Democratic committees brought suit against the Republican National Committee to ensure it couldn’t again use such methods anywhere. For nearly 40 years – through amendments and challenges – the resulting consent decree helped curtail voter suppression tactics .

After the decree’s expiration in 2018, Republicans ramped up their recruitment of poll watchers for the 2020 presidential election. After his loss in that election, Trump led a campaign aimed at discrediting the vote’s legitimacy, claiming fraud and irregularities that he’s been consistently unable to prove .

Since winning in 2024, Trump has led a comprehensive effort to discredit and suppress mail voting . And the Department of Justice, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon posted on X, has a “ plan to send 1,000 federal election monitors to select locations around the country to observe the general election in November. This will be the largest monitoring effort in @theJusticeDept history!”
In addition to those efforts, CNN reports that “ the Republican National Committee is training new ‘special monitors’ to scrutinize voting machines.”

This November, Republican tactics in 1981 are worth remembering. They demonstrate that the safeguarding of polling places from allegedly fraudulent voters and of public places from supposedly threatening people of color share not only a logic.
This story is an updated version of an article originally published Aug. 10, 2020.

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: In Eastlake, a shuttered Starbucks is turning into gold as Bellevue Rare Coins moves in
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: One of the great under-told Seattle stories of the 21st century is how the city’s economic tides and entrepreneurial currents have filled the spaces left behind by the retreat of its hometown coffee giant.

One recent example is in the Central District at 23rd and Jackson where cafe and job training venture Coffee TAB is now serving in a space Starbucks exited over public safety concerns in a neighborhood it had been so proud to debut in decades earlier. On Capitol Hill, there are tacos on Broadway and pet supplies on E Olive Way .

The city’s next post-SBUX regeneration will come below Capitol Hill in Eastlake where a former Starbucks cafe is lined up to provide a new service in the neighborhood dealing in precious metals, numismatics, fine watches, and jewelry along the main drag.
The opening will also be a return to the city for a company with a long history of serving the rare coin, and gold and silver needs of Seattle customers.
City paperwork shows a new outlet for Bellevue Rare Coins is being planned for a change of use in the 2300 block Eastlake Ave E space where Starbucks shuttered its neighborhood outlet.

Bellevue Rare Coins offers precious metal dealing, numismatic services, estate purchasing, and custom jewelry care across Puget Sound locations in Bellevue, Issaquah, Lynnwood, and Tacoma… and, soon, Eastlake.

The shop won’t be the first Bellevue Rare Coins located in Seattle. In 2022 , the company shuttered its West Seattle flagship after being unable to upgrade the security of its longtime shop following an armed robbery at the outlet.

With spot gold and silver trading at highs, industry reports detail storefronts like BRC shifting heavily toward consumer selling rather than buying. Meanwhile, precious metals and estate appraisals rely, um, heavily on customers transporting high-value items to the store. While Eastlake Ave E is a big construction mess right now , the corridor is being reconfigured for transit, driver, and pedestrian safety improvements with a planned launch of a new RapidRide J line in 2027.

The big driver? The property has a surface parking lot and isn’t far off I-5. And it was for sale. Records show corporations related to the company behind the purchase of the Eastlake parcel for $2 million in August.

Back then, that was about 500 ounces of shiny gold. By next summer — if industry forecasts hold — those ounces will be worth around $2.5 million. There’s no telling if Eastlake real estate will keep up.

Meanwhile, some Starbucks holes take longer to patch. One of its biggest is on Melrose and Pine where the company suddenly closed its $20 million+ Capitol Hill roastery. That space has now been empty and shuttered for over a year .

articles.title: Zahilay Proposes Advancing RapidRide R Funding to Spur Bus Upgrades
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: King County Executive Girmay Zahilay has proposed to advance a significant portion of the funding for Seattle's RapidRide R Line , in the hopes of achieving an "accelerated delivery timeline." The project will run between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach and replace the current Route 7. It is currently slated for a 2032 ribbon-cutting, which Zahilay has touted the possibility of moving up.
However, early designs for the R Line are seeing pushback, over changes that are seen as degrading an existing bus route that is already one of King County Metro's busiest.

Out of the R Line's total $91.2 million expected cost, $64.4 million would be advanced into the current 2026-2027 budget, if the County Council signs off on Zahilay's "omnibus" budget proposal as transmitted last month. That cash advance comes in the wake of a decision to not seek federal dollars for the R Line, something that reflects a bleak federal transit environment and also a hope that Metro would be nimbler without federal strings attached.

Metro is planning R Line upgrades in conjunction with major planned repaving work on Rainier Avenue being advanced by the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). An overhaul of the corridor from S Jackson Street to S Walden Street in Mount Baker, being paired with maintenance work on S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, is expected to cost the city more than $100 million and provides an opportunity to include changes like new bus lanes, enhanced sidewalks, or separated bike facilities.

"Our goal in accelerating this funding is to build a strong partnership with SDOT and bolster our shared commitment to this project," Callie Craighead, Zahilay's press secretary, told The Urbanist . "King County Metro and the Seattle Department of Transportation are actively working to develop plans for shared investments along the RapidRide R alignment that minimize construction and roadway impacts, save costs, and support an accelerated delivery timeline. We heard from SDOT that they would like King County to make a stronger funding commitment to the project to avoid another situation where uncertain funding leads to delays or pauses in the project."
As a bus route that bisects Zahilay's former county council district, the new County Executive has turned the corridor upgrade into one of his administration's major transit priorities.

"I'm challenging Metro to do anything in our power to work with the City of Seattle to build a quality product as fast as possible," Zahilay said at a Metro open house for the project in August. "Every single weekday people are relying on this [route], so I wouldn't be advocating for a RapidRide R on a personal level if I didn't know that it was going to make the service better."

The Route 7 currently carries more than 11,000 daily riders on weekdays, making it the busiest route in Metro's network that never leaves the City of Seattle. With light rail running along MLK Way in parallel with the Route 7 for much of its route, the bus is often the choice for shorter local trips, or downtown trips for riders who aren't able to easily get to the faster train.

Officials hope the R Line will be significantly faster than Route 7, in part due to bus stop consolidation. But when early design concepts presented at open houses this summer showed that a significant number of existing bus stops were on the table to be eliminated with the conversion to the R Line, concerns mounted that current 7 riders would have longer walks to access transit than they do today, and people with disabilities might lose access altogether.

The maps that Metro recently presented resurfaced some of the same issues that plagued the project in its first iteration, before being officially put back on the shelf in 2021 due to financial constraints.

"A RapidRide would reduce the number of stops on the route, which would make it harder for people who currently rely on their local route," Urbanist contributor Ashley Archibald wrote that year , in a story that references many of the same issues that community members are bringing up now.

In the name of speeding up trips, Metro's initial concept would have consolidated 67 stops along the entire corridor into 45, counting both northbound and southbound trips. Along the northern segment of Rainier Avenue, for example, three northbound stops between Judkins Park Station and 12th Avenue would be converted into just one stop at S Dearborn Street. Heading south from Judkins Park, riders would have only one opportunity – at S Walker Street – to deboard before getting to Mount Baker Station.

Estimates produced by Metro in 2020 showed a travel time savings of 7.3 minutes to 11.7 minutes with the R Line during peak hours by 2040, but a big portion of those savings were expected to come from bus lanes that SDOT has actually implemented along some segments of Rainier Avenue since that time. Metro has not yet released any updated time savings data for its current concepts that reflect the gains that have already been made in reliability for the 7.

"There's a lot of folks using the bus to travel locally within Rainier Valley, and commuting to downtown as efficiently as possible is not necessarily the top priority for a lot of folks who are using transit right now on this road," Anna Zivarts, founder and executive director of the Nondrivers Alliance, told The Urbanist .

This past weekend, Zivarts hosted a Route 7 ride with local mobility advocates and elected officials to present them with an up-close view of who is actually using the bus today. In attendance were State Senator Rebecca Saldaña and Port Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa – both are campaigning to become the next King County Councilmember for District 2 – as well as Seattle Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and 37th Legislative District state house candidate Kelabe Tewolde. The event was timed with the annual Week Without Driving .

Rinck noted that Rainier Avenue was included in her "Better Bus Lanes" budget proposal that was unanimously approved last year, along with the successful Denny Way bus lanes that were installed this summer .

"We've made progress on bus lanes. We now need the frequency to match the need, and so that is why I'm really excited about RapidRide R, particularly from the frequency components that will come with it," Rinck told The Urbanist following the ridealong. "I have some outstanding concerns about the stop elimination plan, and I'm curious to learn more about what the county is thinking on that front. But the city is going to need to be a partner in those infrastructure improvements to support that project coming online. I'm really committed to working with riders and future riders of the 7/RapidRide R to make sure that it's meeting community needs."

Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist that the agency is still actively developing an updated proposal for RapidRide R, ahead of a potential King County Council vote confirming the route's alignment and planned stop locations next month.

"Rescoping work for the R Line is still underway," Sanders said. "Metro is using what we’ve been hearing from the community, along with updated technical analysis, to help identify the highest-priority elements of the project. Because the corridor and travel patterns have changed since the original concept was developed, this step is critical to making sure the final design reflects current needs."

While the proposals presented this summer weren't much changed from the previous iteration of the R Line, the refreshed plans may be more aligned with current needs along the corridor and more responsive to critiques from riders.

"While we are still compiling all of the input, we have heard strong support for increased investment in transportation infrastructure in South Seattle and that riders want fast, reliable transit service throughout the Rainier Valley. We are also hearing that stop locations and walking distance are important to Route 7 riders," Sanders continued.
Craighead said that Zahilay's office has been engaged with Metro when it comes to what that updated proposal looks like.

"Our team is actively working with King County Metro to develop a RapidRide R alignment proposal to transmit to the King County Council," Craighead told The Urbanist . "Executive Zahilay and members of his staff joined open houses about the project this summer to hear community feedback directly and are working with Metro to incorporate that feedback into the proposal. Delivering long-promised and long-overdue transit investments to South Seattle continues to be a priority for the Executive."

It will ultimately fall on Zahilay's office and the Metro team to thread the needle on what is already an intensely beloved bus, even if frequent bus bunching and overcrowding does get on riders' nerves.

"If we're trying to entice people into riding transit who have other options already, that's a different priority than meeting the needs of people who are already relying on transit and don't have other options in the Rainier Valley, and that's a very large population here," Zivarts said. "And so I worry with this RapidRide proposal, it's focused more on the theoretical person who might be enticed to ride transit if their commute was shorter, versus the people who need it to get to the grocery store, the pharmacy, or whatever they need to do along this corridor."

Dälek, Lamarr Family Values Oct 8 America’s most uncompromising hip-hop group, New Jersey’s Dälek, have been enlightening and blowing minds since 1998. A staunch advocate for POC’s rights, MC Dälek (aka Will Brooks) trenchantly rails against oppression and strife, from now to centuries back, with an authoritative bellow and a conspiratorial sneer while he and producer/instrumentalist Mike Manteca fuse industrial noise, drone, and funk into towers of sonic power. Their newest album, 2026’s Brilliance of a Falling Moon , takes a flamethrower to the fa$cist ruling class. This decade’s awful times have motivated Dälek to rise to even higher heights of lyrical causticity and sonic brutality. After 28 years of public service in the underground-hip-hop trenches, they’ve proved themselves to be the true heirs to Public Enemy’s crown. ( Funhouse, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

Gary Bartz NTU Troop Oct 11 Earshot Jazz Festival did us a solid by booking Gary Bartz NTU Troop. The iconic 86-year-old jazz saxophonist has played with Charles Mingus, Miles Davis (see Live-Evil ), McCoy Tyner, and other legends, and he still sounds vital. Launched in 1969, NTU Troop—featuring the late, great Andy Bey on vocals—helped to lay the foundation for what’s become known as spiritual jazz. Their blend of soul, funk, African folk music, hard bop, and free jazz resulted in several albums that stimulate both body and mind. Currently, Bartz is supporting a serene, uplifting new album he cut with London-based Your Brother’s Keeper, Where Rivers Meet . One of Bartz’s most indelible songs is 1977’s “Music Is My Sanctuary,” and it behooves us to realize that his is ours, too. ( Triple Door, 7:30 pm, all ages ) DAVE SEGAL

somesurprises, Ilyas Ahmed, Morgan Henderson Oct 16 Formerly the bedroom project of singer-songwriter Natasha El-Sergany, somesurprises has evolved through the years into a dynamic duo with synthesist and guitarist Josh Medina, blending soothing folk with electronic elements and shoegaze-inspired fuzz. Their latest EP, Year Without Spring, is appropriately reverbed (which, in my opinion, is a lot of reverb) and will most definitely sound amazing in the Good Shepherd Center’s spacious Chapel Performance Space. They will be joined by Portland-based experimental artist Ilyas Ahmed and multi-instrumentalist and Stranger Genius Award short-lister Morgan Henderson (Blood Brothers, Fleet Foxes). For fans of: Broadcast, La Luz, Mazzy Star, Phoebe Bridgers, and Slowdive. ( Chapel Performance Space, 7:30 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

DJ Shadow Celebrates 30 Years of Endtroducing….. Oct 17 There is a scene in the documentary Scratch that perfectly captures DJ Shadow. He is in the basement of a Davis, California record store. He is sitting cross-legged on the floor, among stacks and stacks of dusty and abandoned records. The ceiling is low. Pipes are visible. The light in this stuffed space has a glow that’s otherworldly. It is indeed spiritual, and this is how his 1996 masterpiece, Endtroducing….. sounds. It’s the spirituality of sampling. This is why his album will never die. It is just too pure to erode or decay like a body. It instead floats in an ether of forgotten songs, singers, riffs, melodies. Both Blackalicious and DJ Shadow formed, along with Latyrx, the foundation of the legendary Bay Area collective Quannum. If Blackalicious were intellectual rappers, DJ Shadow was something of a medium, a person with the powers of clairaudience. ( Paramount Theatre, 8 pm, all ages ) CHARLES MUDEDE

Tyondai Braxton Oct 20 The son of legendary experimental saxophonist Anthony Braxton, Tyondai’s anything but a nepo baby. He’s earned his lofty status in underground music through his exploits in former best band in the omniverse Battles, who took math rock to rarely matched realms of rhythmic complexity, melodic whimsicality, and electronic tomfoolery. Braxton departed Battles in 2010 and since then has been focusing on a solo career that’s veered from vaulting orchestral and electroacoustic composition to abstract electronic music that could discombobulate Autechre fans’ neurons. On Braxton’s mind-bending new album, Splayed Werks , he conjures alien sound worlds that expand the vocabulary of electronic-music composition. This is a rare seated show at Vera, so STFU and listen. ( Vera Project, 7 pm, all ages ) DAVE SEGAL

Debt Rag, Miscomings, DJ Martin Douglas Oct 21 Astute local music critic and DJ Martin Douglas has coordinated another strong bill for his Trick Bag series. Olympia’s premier experimental-rock band, Debt Rag, puts punk and no wave in a cyclotron, resulting in concise, idiosyncratic songs that send diabolical heat and sparks through your sensorium. The trio’s music and lyrics possess the urgency and righteous rage that this perilous timeline demands. Check out their latest album, It Is Clear What’s Going On , for proof. Seattle’s Miscomings seemingly have absorbed the harsh lessons of the legendary No New York comp and transformed them into tracks that come at you like a herd of amphetamine-spiked porcupines, with bonus doses of Minutemen-like funk. Exhilaration awaits you. ( Sunset Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala With Salt-N-Pepa Oct 22 MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala is probably your only chance to see the queens of hip-hop, Salt-N-Pepa, at a venue this tiny (unless you time-travel back to 1986). The duo, with DJ Spinderella, of course, will perform classics like “Whatta Man,” “Shoop,” “Let’s Talk About Sex,” and “None of Your Business” at the 250-capacity Sky Church. I really hope they also play a few songs from their criminally underrated 1997 album Brand New , which is rich with wordplay and glossy ’90s production, in the same vein as Lil’ Kim’s Hard Core . And look, I recognize that the $250 ticket price is no small thing, but if you’ve ever paid Ticketmaster/Live Nation hundreds of dollars, don’t think twice about supporting the MOPOP with their future exhibitions, youth education programs, and community initiatives. ( MOPOP, 8:30 pm, 21+ ) AUDREY VANN

Ken Ishii, Cory Simpson Oct 25 Ken Ishii was the first Japanese solo electronic-music producer I got hip to, thanks to his 1995 album Flare dazzling me with its ingenious textures and dynamic rhythms. Throughout the ’90s, Ishii released a grip of phenomenal records in which IDM, techno, funky breaks, and ambient converged into fascinating hybrids. Shamefully, I lost track of him in the ’00s, but, whoa, Ken’s still creating and DJing like a madman, including a 2019 collab with Detroit techno legend Jeff Mills. Whether he’s performing his own cuts or spinning others’ in his wide-ranging sets, Ishii manifests a distinctive brand of dance-floor hypnosis. At Substation, he’ll be DJing, along with Cory Simpson, a prime mover in Seattle’s techno scene who heads the Depth crew. ( Substation, 7 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

The Chicks Oct 25–26 Do you remember where you were when the Chicks premiered “Not Ready to Make Nice”? I was 10 years old, sitting on the couch getting ready to leave for school when it first played on VH1. While I won’t pretend I understood the conflict at hand, I had seen ex-fans burning their CDs on the news, and I didn’t like the outrage toward the three sparkly women who made the only country music I liked. “Not Ready to Make Nice” isn’t just a courageous political statement that doubled down on their criticism of Bush, but it’s an excellent pop song. Even when I was 10, with almost no understanding of politics, the bubbling rage and frustration carried through and inspired me. And, in a time when artists are still being punished for speaking out against war (see: Macklemore, who was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour last month for advocating against Palestinian genocide), the legacy of the Chicks’ Taking the Long Way is a reminder that being on the right side of history is always worth it, even if it means loss of money or an audience you didn’t want in the first place. The trio will celebrate the 20th anniversary of the album by playing it in its entirety for two consecutive nights at Benaroya Hall. ( Benaroya Hall, 8:30 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

Frankie Cosmos Oct 26 Wanna feel old? It’s been 10 years since Greta Kline, aka Frankie Cosmos, released her 2016 studio album Next Thing , which contains some of her most well-known songs, including “Fool,” “Sappho,” and “Outside With the Cuties.” The dreamy, wistful record features influences from poet Frank O’Hara and musician Arthur Russell, with Kline’s floaty vocals and contemplative lyrics layered over soft synths. It packs the emotional punch of a coming-of-age film into the span of 28 minutes and 28 seconds and defined my 20s—in fact, I am having an existential spiral realizing that it’s been a decade since I attended the Vera Project show for Frankie Cosmos’s West Coast tour promoting this album alongside former Seattle favorites iji (now based in Los Angeles). Kline and her band will return to Seattle to celebrate Next Thing ’s anniversary at the Crocodile, with an opening set by hometown heroes Coral Grief, and I fully expect it to heal me. ( Crocodile, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

Kacey Musgraves, the Brudi Brothers Oct 26–27 I’ve been a fan of Dolly Parton’s spiritual successor Kacey Musgraves since her 2013 single “Follow Your Arrow,” and it’s been a treat to watch her career evolve over the years. Her bittersweet latest album, Middle of Nowhere , finds her deep in her single era, evoking both liminal spaces and her Texan roots—the title comes from a sign she spotted in her hometown that read, “​​Golden, Texas: Somewhere in the middle of nowhere.” It’s by turns horny, as on the touch-starved bop “Dry Spell” (“Ain’t nobody’s tool up in my shed / Ain’t nobody’s boots under my bed”), and heartbreaking, as on the ballad “Hell on Me.” She also works out a 15-year feud with country star Miranda Lambert on the remix in their duet “Horses and Divorces”: “It’s all whiskey under the bridge.” Seattle-based sibling busker trio the Brudi Brothers will kick off Musgraves’s show at Climate Pledge Arena. ( Climate Pledge Arena, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

beabadoobee, Wisp Oct 29 I’m hard-pressed to think of many artists who reinvent themselves as effortlessly and confidently as Beatrice Laus, better known by her stage name beabadoobee. The Filipino British singer-songwriter rose to fame with her debut single, “Coffee,” which went viral on YouTube in 2017 and blew up even more after it was sampled on Canadian rapper ​​Powfu’s TikTok-popular 2019 song “Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head).” Two years after her indie-pop album This Is How Tomorrow Moves , she’s adopting an edgier, grungier sound with her new album Pylon , which incorporates ’90s alt influences and enlists Hayley Williams, Pinegrove’s Evan Stephens Hall, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates as collaborators. Laus’s ethereal vocals recall the Cranberries’ Dolores O’Riordan over fuzzy, shoegaze-tinged guitars, simmering with heartbreak and nostalgia—the album gets its title from the pylon towers she’d gaze at out the window while homesick on tour. Up-and-coming nu-gaze artist Wisp will join her on her first arena tour. ( Climate Pledge, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

Rebecca Black, BAYLI Oct 30 Rebecca Black has successfully shed the skin of her notoriously cringe viral bop “Friday.” Today, her public persona leans into her status as a queer icon, hyperpop sensation, and collaborator of genre rule-breakers like Dylan Brady (100 gecs), Big Freedia, and Dorian Electra. On her sophomore album, Age of the Exhibitionist , she harmonizes about kink and pleasure à la Madonna’s Erotica . Explaining to Out Magazine her hopes for the album, Black said, “I hope [listeners] sweat, I hope they fuck, I hope they do everything they need to do. There really is a song for everything on this record.” Brooklyn-based artist BAYLI will open with her signature blend of club, rap, and pop bangers. ( Showbox, 7 pm, all ages ) AUDREY VANN

Styled by the Streets: Black Women in Hip-Hop Fashion Ongoing When I think of the most important fashion moments in music, I think of Lil’ Kim’s purple pasty ensemble (and other iconic monochromatic looks), Missy Elliott’s inflatable trash bag suit, Salt-N-Pepa’s matching kufis paired with spandex bodysuits, and TLC’s fishnet tops that spell out their band name. Black female hip-hop artists take fashion risks when others won’t, and continue to innovate when other artists imitate (summed up by the Lil’ Kim lyric, “I used to wear Moschino, but every bitch got it / Now I rock colorful minks because my pockets stay knotted”). The Museum of Pop Culture’s newest exhibit celebrates this history, showcasing over 30 artifacts—that’s wigs, nails, clothing, and accessories—from across time, with pieces worn by icons like Mary J. Blige, Lil’ Kim, Cardi B, and Doja Cat. ( MOPOP ) AUDREY VANN

Kelly Bjork: Lunacy Through Oct 28 Kelly Bjork’s work has always been about tenderness and the intimacy of interior spaces, but there’s another narrative threading through it: a personal reckoning. Their first solo show at J. Rinehart, Swimming Naked , marked the arrival of an imagery that was explicit, fleshy, and decidedly queer. In their new exhibition, Lunacy , that blissful raunch gives way to something darker, as Bjork dances with literal demons and confronts the spiritual, emotional, and physical disruptions of perimenopause. The work remains rife with impeccable patterns and intimate details sprinkled like Easter eggs throughout, but now those details reveal something grittier, wilder, and more brutally intimate than what’s come before. ( J. Rinehart Gallery ) AMANDA MANITACH

Actualize AiR Takes Over The Stranger Offices Oct 8 The love train for our 2026 Genius Award winners isn’t stopping anytime soon. On October 8, we’re letting Visual Arts Geniuses, Actualize AiR, take over the third floor of The Stranger offices for Capitol Hill Art Walk. Come! It will be so great! We told them they can do whatever the fuck they want, and since Actualize is a by-artists for-artists organization that encourages makers to take risks with their work, I, for one, can’t wait to see what they come up with. (Just please don’t break anything on my desk.) Another reason to visit us during art walk: candy! Stranger Marketing Manager Evanne Hall will be curating a Cursed Candy table full of wicked delights (juice-filled wax bottles and fish-flavored candy canes, anyone?), and I will be doing my damndest to make candy corn lovers out of anyone brave enough, with my candy corn smorgasbord. If you don’t like candy corn, you just haven’t had it in the right circumstances! Let me help you! Candy corn forever! ( The Stranger, the entrance is located on 11th Ave E between the Gemini Room and Chophouse Row, 5–8 pm ) MEGAN SELING

Refract: The Seattle Glass Experience Oct 15–18 If you’ve ever yearned to deepen your knowledge of the region’s glass scene, gather with glassholes, or dabble in the hot shop yourself, let Refract be your guide. The annual festival takes place at galleries, museums, and studios across the greater Seattle area. Sample the hottest young glass artists in town (like Yale Wolf, Megan Stelljes, and Henry Jackson-Spieker) in Refract: Local Frequencies at The Space Columbia City, get hands-on making your own decorative autumnal squash at SLU’s Seattle Glassblowing Studio, or get downward-dog amid Chihuly’s many-tentacled splendors during a yoga class at the Chihuly Garden and Glass Museum. My top picks, however, are the intimate artist open studio sessions with masters of the craft like Carol Milne, Morgan Madison, and Weston Lambert. ( Various locations ) AMANDA MANITACH

Melissa Messer Through Oct 31 Melissa Messer describes her practice and work as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” I might add Albers to the mix: her approach to color is technical and clever and makes the eyeballs vibrate with a kind of ocular orgasm. But she’s right about Rothko, because her use of hue is almost spiritual in its ability to overwhelm. She is also a preeminent figurative painter, using the human body as an armature upon which to drape shades of deciduous greens, burnt orange, and acid gold. Beneath all that color, however, the figures hold their own. Messer paints to convey intimacy—the kind that comes from knowing the closeness of a body from innumerable hours of holding, caring, carrying, or resting. That feeling is palpable in the heavy limbs of the mothers, friends, and others who populate her canvases. They loom, stark and monumental, bodies dissolving into the color fields that surround them. ( Spectrum Fine Art ) AMANDA MANITACH

Surge: A Geography of Flow Through Jan 10 It’s fitting that Surge, an exhibition that pairs visual artists with scientists to make work about climate change, takes place at the Museum of Northwest Art, located in La Conner, Washington. Climate change isn’t just a hypothetical in the Skagit basin, a 3,115-square-mile watershed that extends from the Cascades to the Skagit Bay. It’s experienced firsthand as the sea spills over levees, roads go underwater, and the familiar ways of doing things are swept away. This is the fourth iteration of Surge, curated by Chloé Dye Sherpe, and it’s always fascinating to see what happens when artists spend quality time in the trenches with the climatologists, hydrologists, biologists, and governmental policymakers tracking the changes that directly affect our region. This year’s robust roster includes artists working across media, from neon and glass to painting and assemblage: Holly Ballard Martz, Kelsey Fernkopf and Steve Gilbert, Melinda Hurst Frye, Morgan Madison, Steve Jensen, Sue Danielson, and Niki Keenan, to name but a few. ( Museum of Northwest Art ) AMANDA MANITACH

Make Your Own Cursed Lafufu Oct 18 My New Year’s resolution was to make more art in 2026. Not for work, not to sell—I just wanted to prioritize making a mess for no reason other than to have fun. I picked up cross-stitching, got back into block printing, and have become mildly obsessed with making photo zines with the dirtylittlezine.com template. But the most fun art project I’ve done all year has been the Make Your Own Cursed “Lafufu” class at Push/Pull, where you get to make your own freaky, DIY Labubu, that polarizing plush collectible with a plastic face. The session is led by Holly Conrad, who made costumes for Robot Chicken and Guillermo del Toro. At Push/Pull, she dumps a bunch of art supplies on the table—small stuffed critters, polymer clay, glue guns, plastic eyes, fake teeth, sculpting tools, even resin that has to be treated with a UV lamp should you want to make your guy look a little wet or slimy—and as you cut off a stuffie’s face, she shares all her tips of the trade, from the ideal thickness of the clay so your monster’s face isn’t too heavy, to how to get realistic-looking wrinkles around the eyes. I left the three-hour class with a new bestie, a little lion named Meatball who has tentacles and buck teeth. What friend will you make? ( Push/Pull, 2–5 pm ) MEGAN SELING

Melissa King Oct 9 Last year, Top Chef fan favorite and lesbian heartthrob Melissa King released her James Beard Award-winning debut cookbook Cook Like a King . You may recall that she and the show’s host Padma Lakshmi sent the collective sapphic universe into a gay panic with their flirty Instagram banter while simultaneously promoting their books, plus there was a sultry Gomez and Morticia couple costume that ignited dating rumors. (They’re just friends, or so they claim…) Now, King is back with her memoir The Girl Who Became King . The book shares her story of growing up queer in a Shanghainese and Cantonese family in Los Angeles’s Gabriel Valley, her initiation into the high-stakes world of Michelin-starred restaurants, and her Top Chef journey. She’ll share her story with food writer, photographer, designer, and Little Fat Boy blogger Frankie Gaw at this event, hosted by Charlie’s Queer Books at Ballard Homestead. ( Ballard Homestead, 7 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

Seattle Restaurant Week Oct 18–31 Sure, it’s confusing that Seattle Restaurant Week is actually two weeks, but that just means we have twice as much time to pig out on specials from dozens of delicious participating restaurants. And there are some true superstars on the list. Lupe’s Situ Tacos in Ballard will be offering a few different specials, including three of their incredibly crispy tacos, or five taquitos, served alongside a cup of soup, aguas frescas, and baklava for $30. That’s enough food for two! (Though I do hate to share my taquitos.) There’s also Shiro’s Sushi, Marination in Columbia City (and, hell yeah, their special includes malasadas), Kilig, which Stranger contributor Meg van Huygen put on her 2024 Best Restaurants in the Seattle Area list, and Melting Pot in Bellevue. I did not know Melting Pot still existed! The ’90s really are back. (Various locations) MEGAN SELING

Seattle Coffee Festival Oct 24–25 More than two dozen roasters are participating in the Seattle Coffee Festival, and I’m already strategizing how to drink everything without causing my nervous system to collapse on itself. The lineup features Victrola Coffee, Boon Boona, Kuma Coffee, Anchorhead Coffee, Sip House, and Speed Potion, whose iridescent and shimmery packaging makes my heart skip a beat even without the jolt of caffeine. Thankfully, there will be some food to help sop up all the coffee, including 9th and Hennepin Donuts, and treats from the Anh Ơi Bake Shop (read more about them in our November issue!). If they have their fried banana cookies, I’m going to buy up every single one for myself. Sorry. ( Magnuson Park Hangar 30, times vary ) MEGAN SELING
